Frequently asked questions

Have another question? Write to us from the feedback panel inside the platform.

What does the free plan include?
The first subtopic of each topic's summary (across all three units), the first 5 exam questions, a short 5-question daily practice exam, a demo round of the BioMatch game, and a set of basic flashcards. It's enough to understand the quality and format of the product. It's not enough to study for the full exam unit.
Which plan is right for me? U1, U2, U3 or Full Semester?
Unit 1, 2 or 3 Pass ($11.99 each · 60 days): if you only need to pass one exam unit. Full Semester ($24.99 · 6 months): the most popular plan. Buying the three passes separately costs $35.97; with the Semester you pay $24.99 (save $10.98) and have access to everything from day 1. Monthly Plan ($9.99/mo): if you want to try before committing. If you'll study 3+ months, the Semester is better value.
If I buy Unit 1 Pass, can I buy Unit 2 separately later?
Yes, you can buy it later. But buying all three passes separately ($11.99 each) would cost $35.97 total; the Full Semester costs $24.99 (save $10.98). If you're still within the semester, the best option is switching to the Semester from the start or asking us for a proportional upgrade. Write to us from the feedback panel.
Why doesn't the free plan include more?
Because the real value is in the features that save you time and improve your chances of passing: the diagnostic that tells you exactly what you're missing, the personalized plan by exam date, the "What to study today" panel, the pass prediction, unlimited practice exams, and the complete summary. Those features are what justify the payment. If we gave them away, the platform couldn't be sustained.
Does this work for any General Biology course?
The content is designed from the standard university General Biology syllabus (introduction, biomolecules, cell biology, metabolism, photosynthesis and respiration for the first unit; genetic foundations, evolution and biotechnology for the second; origin of life, biological diversity and ecology for the third). These topics are the same across most university General Biology programs. The platform is independent and usable for students from different universities.
Is there a refund if it's not for me?
Yes, on any plan. If within the first 7 days you feel it's not right for you and you haven't used more than 20% of the content, we'll refund 100%, no questions asked. Write to the official email Biomaster.oficial@gmail.com or use the feedback panel in the app. Resetting your game progress does NOT void your right to a refund, but it also doesn't reset the administrative progress record: if you exceeded 20%, that data is registered.
How is my progress saved?
If you register with your email, your progress (diagnostic, study plan, frequent errors, practice exams) is saved in the cloud and synced across devices. If you enter as a guest, progress is saved only in this browser. Progress for each unit is kept separate (what you do in U1 doesn't affect your U2 map).
Does it work on mobile?
Yes. The platform is optimized for mobile, tablet and desktop. Practice exams, games and the study plan work the same on any device.
When is the content updated?
The theoretical summary is updated whenever there are changes in the course program. Practice exams are periodically refreshed with new questions. Official exams (2024, 2025…) are incorporated as they're published, and active-plan subscribers access them at no extra cost during their period.

📘 Unit 1 · General Biology

📚 Theory summary — Unit 1

Topics 1 to 5 of the syllabus: introduction, chemical composition, cell biology, photosynthesis and cellular respiration. Each subtopic includes typical errors, exam keys, and how questions are usually asked.

1
Topic 1. Course introduction
What biology is, characteristics of living things, levels of organization, and scientific method.
T1
⭐ Key: introductory, conceptual block with low technical weight, but often yields quick points on theoretical questions. Master definitions and scientific method.
1.1 Importance of biology as a science
  • Biology is the science that studies life at all levels: from molecules to ecosystems.
  • Contributes to health, agriculture, biotechnology, conservation, and understanding of natural phenomena.
  • Based on empirical evidence and scientific method, not opinions.
  • Key: distinguish basic science (seeks knowledge) from applied science (solves concrete problems).
1.2 Characteristics of living organisms
  • Made of cells: the cell is the structural and functional unit of life.
  • Maintain homeostasis: stable internal conditions despite external changes.
  • Carry out metabolism: set of chemical reactions to obtain and use energy.
  • Grow and develop: increase in size and complexity in a regulated manner.
  • Respond to stimuli: detect and react to environmental changes.
  • Reproduce and inherit: generate offspring with similar genetic material.
  • Evolve: populations change across generations.
  • Error: it's not just "moving" or "breathing"; the combination of all 7 characteristics defines a living organism.
1.3 Fundamental concepts in biology
  • Organism: individual living being.
  • Species: group of organisms that can reproduce with each other and produce fertile offspring.
  • Population: individuals of the same species in the same place and time.
  • Community: different populations coexisting in the same place.
  • Ecosystem: community + abiotic factors (soil, water, climate).
  • Biosphere: all ecosystems on the planet.
1.4 Levels of organization of life
  • Ascending order: atom → molecule → organelle → cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism → population → community → ecosystem → biosphere.
  • Each level has emergent properties that don't appear at the lower level.
  • Key: the cell is the first level where life appears; an isolated atom or molecule is not a living being.
  • Error: confusing the order or skipping the cell level in an ordering question.
1.5 Scientific method: importance and stages
  • Observation: noticing a fact or phenomenon in nature.
  • Question: clear formulation of what is being investigated.
  • Hypothesis: tentative, falsifiable, and testable explanation. Key: must be able to be refuted by experiments.
  • Prediction: expected result if the hypothesis is correct. Usually takes the form "If... then...".
  • Experiment or data collection: test designed with experimental group and control group.
  • Analysis and conclusion: interpretation based on evidence. The hypothesis is supported or rejected, not "proven" as absolute truth.
  • Independent variable: the one the researcher manipulates (cause).
  • Dependent variable: the one that is measured (effect).
  • Control group: group identical to the experimental group except for the variable under study.
  • Scientific theory: broad explanation supported by a large body of evidence (not a "guess"). Error: in everyday language "theory" means assumption; in science it means a well-supported explanation.
  • Scientific law: describes an observed regularity; does not explain why it occurs.
  • How it's asked: "After stating a hypothesis and prediction, what comes next?" → the experiment. "Difference between theory and law" → theory explains, law describes.
2
Topic 2. Chemical composition of living things
Bioelements, bonds, water, pH, biomolecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids).
T2
⭐ Key: high-yield exam topic. Master chemical bonds, water properties, pH, and especially the four biomolecules with their monomers and functions.
2.1.1 Chemical elements and inorganic compounds
  • Primary bioelements (CHONPS): carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur. Make up ~96% of the mass of living things.
  • Secondary bioelements: Ca, Na, K, Mg, Cl. Essential ions in small quantities.
  • Trace elements: Fe, Cu, Zn, Mn, I... present in traces but indispensable (e.g., Fe in hemoglobin, I in thyroid).
  • Key inorganic compounds: water, mineral salts, gases (O₂, CO₂).
  • Key: carbon is central due to its ability to form 4 bonds and long chains, the basis of all organic biomolecules.
2.1.2 Molecules and chemical bonds
  • Ionic bond: one atom donates electrons, another gains them. E.g.: NaCl. Soluble in water, conducts electricity in solution.
  • Nonpolar covalent bond: electrons shared equally. E.g.: C-H, C-C. Small electronegativity difference.
  • Polar covalent bond: electrons shared unequally. E.g.: O-H in water. Creates dipoles.
  • Hydrogen bond: weak attraction between H already bonded to an electronegative atom (O, N, F) and another nearby electronegative atom. Individually weak, collectively decisive.
  • Key: hydrogen bonds are responsible for most of water's properties and for maintaining the DNA double helix.
  • Error: confusing "polar covalent" with "ionic." The polar bond shares (unequally), the ionic bond transfers.
2.1.3 Chemistry of water
  • It is polar (O partially negative, H partially positive).
  • Cohesion: water molecules attract each other via hydrogen bonds → surface tension.
  • Adhesion: water sticks to polar surfaces → capillarity (rises through thin tubes, essential in plants).
  • High specific heat: absorbs a lot of heat before raising temperature → stabilizes temperature of organisms and oceans.
  • High heat of vaporization: requires much energy to evaporate → cooling by sweating.
  • Anomalous density: ice is less dense than liquid water → floats, insulates bodies of water, allows life under ice.
  • "Universal" solvent: dissolves polar and ionic substances. Hydrophobic (nonpolar) substances do not dissolve.
  • Exam key: almost all these properties are explained by hydrogen bonds.
2.1.4 Acids, bases, and pH
  • pH measures the concentration of H⁺ ions (hydronium H₃O⁺) in a solution.
  • Scale 0-14: 0 = very acidic, 7 = neutral, 14 = very basic.
  • Each unit is 10 times: pH 3 is 10 times more acidic than pH 4 and 100 times more acidic than pH 5.
  • Acid: releases H⁺ in solution (HCl).
  • Base: accepts H⁺ or releases OH⁻ (NaOH).
  • Buffer: system that resists pH changes. E.g.: bicarbonate/carbonic acid in blood.
  • Error: "pH 3 is twice as acidic as pH 4." No: it is 10 times more acidic (logarithmic scale).
2.2.1 Carbohydrates
  • Main function: quick energy and structure.
  • Monosaccharides: basic unit. Glucose, fructose, galactose, ribose (in RNA), deoxyribose (in DNA).
  • Disaccharides: two monosaccharides joined by a glycosidic bond. Sucrose (glucose+fructose), lactose (glucose+galactose), maltose (glucose+glucose).
  • Polysaccharides:
    • Starch: energy reserve in plants.
    • Glycogen: energy reserve in animals (liver and muscle).
    • Cellulose: structural component of plant cell walls. Humans cannot digest it.
    • Chitin: exoskeleton of arthropods and cell wall of fungi.
  • Key: starch = plant, glycogen = animal, cellulose = plant wall, chitin = arthropods/fungi.
  • Error: confusing glycogen (animal reserve) with cellulose (plant structure).
2.2.2 Lipids
  • Common characteristic: hydrophobic (do not dissolve in water) due to their long nonpolar regions.
  • Triglycerides (fats and oils): glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Function: concentrated energy reserve.
  • Saturated vs unsaturated: saturated without double bonds (solid at room temperature, animal fats). Unsaturated with double bonds (liquid, vegetable oils).
  • Phospholipids: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate group. Amphipathic: hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail. Form bilayers → cell membranes.
  • Steroids: 4 carbon rings. Cholesterol, sex hormones (estrogen, testosterone), cortisol.
  • Waxes: waterproofing agents (plant cuticle, feathers).
  • Key: phospholipids form bilayers because they are amphipathic.
  • Error: "lipids are polymers." They are not: they are not formed by repeating monomers like carbohydrates or proteins.
2.2.3 Proteins
  • Monomer: amino acid (20 different ones in living things). Each with an amino group, carboxyl group, and variable R group.
  • Peptide bond: joins the carboxyl group of one amino acid with the amino group of the next, releasing water (dehydration synthesis).
  • Primary structure: amino acid sequence.
  • Secondary structure: alpha helix or beta pleated sheet, maintained by hydrogen bonds between carbonyls and aminos.
  • Tertiary structure: full 3D folding of the chain, maintained by interactions between R groups (disulfide bridges, ionic, hydrophobic, hydrogen bonds).
  • Quaternary structure: joining of several polypeptide chains (e.g.: hemoglobin = 4 subunits).
  • Denaturation: loss of 3D structure due to heat, extreme pH, or chemical agents. The protein loses its function.
  • Functions: enzymes (catalysis), structural (keratin, collagen), transport (hemoglobin), defense (antibodies), signaling (hormones like insulin), motor (actin, myosin).
  • Key: function depends on shape; shape depends on amino acid sequence.
  • Error: "a denatured protein only changes its sequence." No: the sequence (primary structure) doesn't change; what is lost is the folding.
2.2.4 Nucleic acids
  • Monomer: nucleotide = nitrogenous base + sugar (pentose) + phosphate group.
  • Bases:
    • Purines (2 rings): adenine (A), guanine (G).
    • Pyrimidines (1 ring): cytosine (C), thymine (T, DNA only), uracil (U, RNA only).
  • DNA: sugar = deoxyribose, double antiparallel strand helix, bases A-T and C-G via hydrogen bonds.
  • RNA: sugar = ribose, single strand, bases A-U and C-G.
  • DNA function: store genetic information.
  • RNA function: intermediary and executor (mRNA transcribes, tRNA transports amino acids, rRNA forms ribosome).
  • Key: base pairing A-T (DNA) or A-U (RNA), C-G always.
  • Error: including T in RNA or U in DNA.
3
Topic 3. Cell biology
Cell theory, prokaryote vs eukaryote, organelles, membrane, transport, osmosis and cell junctions.
T3
⭐ Key: topic with the most questions in U1. Master prokaryote/eukaryote differences, organelle functions, and especially transport types and osmosis.
3.1.1 Cell theory
  • All living things are made up of one or more cells.
  • The cell is the structural and functional unit of life.
  • Every cell comes from a pre-existing cell (Virchow).
  • Key: cell theory was built on contributions from Schleiden (plants), Schwann (animals), and Virchow (origin).
3.1.2 Characteristics common to all cells
  • Plasma membrane that separates them from their environment.
  • Cytoplasm with aqueous cytosol.
  • Ribosomes to synthesize proteins.
  • Genetic material (DNA).
  • Ability to obtain energy and reproduce.
3.1.3 Prokaryotes vs eukaryotes
  • Prokaryotes: no defined nucleus (DNA free in nucleoid), no membrane-bound organelles, smaller ribosomes (70S), generally unicellular. Bacteria and archaea.
  • Eukaryotes: true nucleus surrounded by nuclear envelope, membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, etc.), 80S ribosomes. Plants, animals, fungi, protists.
  • Size: prokaryotes 1-10 µm, eukaryotes 10-100 µm.
  • Key: "no defined nucleus" is the most commonly tested difference.
  • Error: saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes. They do, but they are different (70S).
3.1.4.1 The nucleus
  • Contains most of the cell's DNA.
  • Nuclear envelope: double membrane with nuclear pores that regulate passage of large molecules.
  • Nucleolus: dense internal region where ribosomes are synthesized.
  • Chromatin: DNA + proteins (histones) in uncondensed state during interphase.
3.1.4.2 Endomembrane system
  • Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER): with ribosomes attached. Synthesizes proteins that will be secreted or go to membranes.
  • Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER): without ribosomes. Lipid synthesis, detoxification, Ca²⁺ storage.
  • Golgi apparatus: receives vesicles from the ER, modifies, packages, and routes proteins to their destination. "Packaging center."
  • Lysosomes (animals): vesicles with digestive enzymes, break down macromolecules and old organelles.
  • Vacuoles (plants and protists): storage, maintenance of turgor.
  • Key: the typical flow is RER → vesicles → Golgi → vesicles → membrane or final destination.
3.1.4.3 Other key organelles
  • Mitochondria: double membrane (inner membrane with cristae), inner matrix. Site of cellular respiration and ATP production. Has its own DNA.
  • Chloroplast (plants and algae): double membrane + thylakoids (internal sacs where the light reactions occur) and stroma (where the Calvin cycle occurs). Has its own DNA.
  • Ribosomes: no membrane. Synthesize proteins. Free in cytosol or attached to RER.
  • Peroxisomes: degradation of hydrogen peroxide and oxidation of fatty acids.
  • Key: mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA → endosymbiotic theory.
3.1.4.4 Surface specializations
  • Cell wall: cellulose in plants, chitin in fungi, peptidoglycan in bacteria. Provides shape and protection.
  • Glycocalyx: carbohydrate layer on animal cell surface. Cell recognition.
  • Cilia: short and numerous. Movement of fluids or of the cell.
  • Flagella: long and sparse. Cell movement (sperm, bacteria).
  • Microvilli: projections that increase absorption surface (intestine).
3.1.4.5 Cytoskeleton
  • Network of protein fibers that gives shape, support, and enables movement.
  • Microfilaments (actin): muscle contraction, cell division.
  • Microtubules (tubulin): mitotic spindle, intracellular transport, cilia and flagella.
  • Intermediate filaments (keratin, etc.): mechanical resistance.
3.2.1 Plasma membrane model
  • Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972).
  • Phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic heads facing outward, hydrophobic tails facing inward.
  • Cholesterol: interspersed among phospholipids, regulates fluidity.
  • Integral (transmembrane) proteins: span the bilayer. Function as channels, carriers, receptors.
  • Peripheral proteins: on one face of the membrane. Support and signaling functions.
  • Glycoproteins and glycolipids: with carbohydrates, used for cell recognition.
  • Selectively permeable: allows some substances through but not others.
3.2.2.1 Passive transport (no ATP required)
  • Simple diffusion: movement of molecules down a concentration gradient (high → low). For small nonpolar molecules (O₂, CO₂).
  • Facilitated diffusion: down gradient, but uses carrier proteins or channels (for ions, glucose).
  • Osmosis: diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane, from lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration.
  • Key: in passive transport ATP is never used.
3.2.2.2 Active transport (requires ATP)
  • Primary active: uses ATP directly. E.g.: Na⁺/K⁺ pump (pumps out 3 Na⁺, brings in 2 K⁺ per ATP).
  • Secondary active: uses the gradient generated by another active transport (cotransport).
  • Endocytosis: the cell takes in material by engulfing it with membrane. Phagocytosis (solids), pinocytosis (liquids), receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • Exocytosis: the cell releases material by vesicle fusion with the membrane.
  • Error: "facilitated diffusion uses ATP." No: it uses proteins but is passive, goes down the gradient.
3.2.3 Types of osmotic solutions
  • Isotonic: same solute concentration on both sides → no net water flow.
  • Hypotonic: lower concentration outside → water enters the cell. Red blood cells: hemolysis. Plants: turgor (cell wall prevents bursting).
  • Hypertonic: higher concentration outside → water leaves the cell. Red blood cells: crenation (shrink). Plants: plasmolysis (membrane separates from wall).
  • Key: water always moves toward where there is more solute.
  • Error: confusing "hypo" with "hyper" relative to the cell. Remember: hypotonic = cell swells, hypertonic = cell shrinks.
3.2.5 Cell junctions
  • Tight junctions: seal the space between cells (impermeable). E.g.: intestinal epithelium.
  • Adherens junctions and desmosomes: provide mechanical resistance. E.g.: skin, cardiac muscle.
  • Gap junctions: channels that allow passage of ions and small molecules between neighboring cells.
  • Plasmodesmata (plants): equivalent to gap junctions in plants, pass through the cell wall.
4
Topic 4. Fundamentals of metabolism
Thermodynamics, ATP, redox, enzymes, regulation.
T4
⭐ Key: conceptual foundation for photosynthesis and respiration. Mastering enzymes (active site, inhibition, factors) usually gives easy points.
3.3.1 Energy and laws of thermodynamics
  • First law: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transformed.
  • Second law: in every transformation, some energy is dispersed as heat; the entropy (disorder) of the universe increases.
  • Living things do not violate the second law: they maintain internal order through continuous energy input while increasing disorder in their surroundings.
  • Energy flow: Sun → producers (plants) → consumers → decomposers. Energy flows unidirectionally; nutrients are recycled.
3.3.2 Exergonic and endergonic reactions
  • Exergonic (ΔG < 0): releases energy, spontaneous. E.g.: ATP hydrolysis, cellular respiration.
  • Endergonic (ΔG > 0): requires energy, non-spontaneous. E.g.: protein synthesis, photosynthesis.
  • Coupling: the cell couples exergonic reactions (ATP→ADP) with endergonic ones so the latter can occur.
  • Key: ATP is the "currency" of coupling.
3.3.3 ATP, the energy currency
  • ATP = adenosine triphosphate: adenosine (adenine+ribose) + 3 phosphate groups.
  • The bonds between phosphates are "high-energy": when the terminal one is hydrolyzed (ATP → ADP + Pi), ~7.3 kcal/mol are released.
  • ATP is not "stored" in large quantities; it is continuously synthesized and consumed.
  • ATP synthesis: ADP + Pi + energy → ATP. Occurs in respiration, photosynthesis, and fermentation.
3.3.4 Redox reactions
  • Oxidation: loss of electrons (also loss of H or gain of O).
  • Reduction: gain of electrons (gain of H or loss of O).
  • Mnemonic: "OIL RIG" — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
  • Carriers: NAD⁺/NADH and NADP⁺/NADPH (accept or donate electrons and H).
  • In metabolism, energy usually "travels" as electrons in these carriers.
3.3.5 Enzymes, coenzymes, and cofactors
  • Enzyme: protein (or catalytic RNA) that speeds up biological reactions without being consumed.
  • Active site: region of the enzyme where the substrate binds.
  • Reduces the activation energy needed for the reaction to occur.
  • Induced fit model: the active site changes slightly when the substrate binds (modern version of the rigid "lock-and-key" model).
  • Specificity: each enzyme recognizes a specific substrate or type of reaction.
  • Cofactors: inorganic ions (Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) that assist the enzyme.
  • Coenzymes: organic molecules (NAD⁺, FAD, vitamins).
  • Competitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds to the active site, competing with the substrate.
  • Noncompetitive inhibition: the inhibitor binds to another site (allosteric) and changes the shape of the active site.
  • Negative feedback: the end product inhibits an enzyme at the beginning of the pathway. Enables regulation.
  • Factors affecting activity: temperature (each enzyme has an optimum), pH (also an optimum), substrate concentration, presence of inhibitors.
  • Enzyme denaturation: heat or extreme pH destroys the 3D shape and the enzyme loses function.
  • How it's asked: "When an inhibitor binds to the active site it's called..." → competitive. "When the end product inhibits an enzyme at the start it's called..." → feedback inhibition.
5
Topic 5. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
Chloroplast, light reactions, Calvin cycle, C3/C4/CAM, glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain, fermentation.
T5
⭐ Key: highest-weight topic in U1. Memorize where each stage occurs, what goes in and what comes out, and ATP yields.
3.4.1 Photosynthesis: the general process
  • General equation: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂.
  • Autotrophic producers (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) capture solar energy and convert it into chemical energy.
  • The oxygen released comes from water, not from CO₂.
  • Two phases: light-dependent reactions (in thylakoids) and Calvin cycle / carbon fixation (in stroma).
3.4.2 Light-dependent reactions
  • Location: thylakoid membrane.
  • Pigments: chlorophyll a (main), chlorophyll b, carotenoids.
  • Photosystem II (P680): absorbs light, excites electrons. Energy is used for water splitting (photolysis): 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ + O₂. This is where oxygen is released.
  • Excited electrons pass through the thylakoid electron transport chain, generating an H⁺ gradient between lumen and stroma.
  • Photosystem I (P700): re-excites electrons, which end up reducing NADP⁺ to NADPH.
  • Chemiosmosis: H⁺ returns to the stroma through ATP synthase, generating ATP.
  • Final products: ATP, NADPH, and O₂.
3.4.3 Carbon fixation reactions (Calvin cycle)
  • Location: chloroplast stroma.
  • Does not directly require light, but uses the ATP and NADPH produced in the light reactions.
  • Stage 1 — Fixation: CO₂ + RuBP (5C) → 2 molecules of 3-PGA (3C). Catalyzed by Rubisco (the most abundant enzyme on Earth).
  • Stage 2 — Reduction: 3-PGA + ATP + NADPH → G3P (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate).
  • Stage 3 — Regeneration: some G3P is used to regenerate RuBP; the rest exits the cycle and forms glucose and other sugars.
  • To produce one glucose (6C), 6 turns of the cycle are needed, using 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.
3.4.4 C3, C4, CAM adaptations
  • C3 (90% of plants): first fixation product is 3-PGA (3C). Efficient in temperate climates, but suffer photorespiration in hot climates (Rubisco fixes O₂ instead of CO₂).
  • C4 (corn, sugarcane): spatially separate initial fixation (in mesophyll cells, with PEP carboxylase) from the Calvin cycle (in bundle sheath cells). Reduces photorespiration. Efficient in hot climates.
  • CAM (cactus, pineapple): temporally separated: open stomata at night to fix CO₂ (stored as malate), perform Calvin cycle during day with stomata closed. Adapted to drought.
  • Key: C4 = spatial separation; CAM = temporal separation.
3.4.6 Chloroplast structure and pigments
  • Double membrane: outer and inner.
  • Thylakoids: flattened internal sacs containing chlorophyll. Stacked to form grana (singular: granum).
  • Stroma: aqueous matrix surrounding the thylakoids. Site of the Calvin cycle.
  • Pigments: chlorophyll a (main, absorbs red and blue, reflects green), chlorophyll b (accessory), carotenoids (yellow/orange, also accessory and antioxidants).
3.5.1 Aerobic cellular respiration — Overview
  • General equation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + ATP.
  • 4 stages: glycolysis → pyruvate oxidation → Krebs cycle → electron transport chain.
  • Typical total yield: ~30–32 ATP per glucose.
  • It is the reverse process of photosynthesis (both are needed in ecosystems).
3.5.2 Glycolysis
  • Location: cytoplasm. Does not require oxygen.
  • 1 glucose (6C) → 2 pyruvate (3C).
  • Investment: 2 ATP. Production: 4 ATP + 2 NADH. Net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
  • Occurs in all organisms (prokaryotes and eukaryotes), aerobic and anaerobic alike.
3.5.2.1 Pyruvate oxidation
  • Location: mitochondrial matrix.
  • Each pyruvate loses one CO₂ and combines with coenzyme A → acetyl-CoA (2C).
  • Per pyruvate: 1 CO₂ + 1 NADH.
  • Per glucose (2 pyruvates): 2 CO₂ + 2 NADH.
3.5.3 Citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle)
  • Location: mitochondrial matrix.
  • Per acetyl-CoA (1 turn): 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 ATP (or GTP) + 2 CO₂.
  • Per glucose (2 turns): 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP + 4 CO₂.
  • This is where complete oxidation of carbon is finished.
3.5.4 Electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation
  • Location: inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).
  • NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain.
  • Electron flow pumps H⁺ from the matrix to the intermembrane space, creating a gradient.
  • O₂ is the final electron acceptor: O₂ + e⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O. This is why we need to breathe oxygen.
  • The H⁺ gradient drives ATP synthase → produces most of the ATP. This is called chemiosmosis.
  • Approximate yield: ~26–28 ATP at this stage.
  • Error: "oxygen produces ATP." No: oxygen accepts electrons; ATP is produced by ATP synthase using the H⁺ gradient.
3.5.5 Fermentation (anaerobic)
  • When it occurs: when no oxygen is available.
  • Main function: regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH, so glycolysis can continue.
  • Lactic acid fermentation: pyruvate + NADH → lactate + NAD⁺. In muscle during intense exercise, in yogurt bacteria.
  • Alcoholic fermentation: pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂ → ethanol + NAD⁺. In yeasts (beer, wine, bread).
  • Total yield: only 2 ATP per glucose (from glycolysis).
  • Key: fermentation does not produce more ATP than glycolysis; it only regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.
⏰ 30 minutes before the exam — The critical minimum
  • Scientific method: after hypothesis and prediction → experiment. Independent variable = cause, dependent variable = effect.
  • Water: its properties come from hydrogen bonds.
  • Biomolecules: Carbohydrates = monosaccharides. Lipids = not polymers, hydrophobic. Proteins = amino acids via peptide bonds. Nucleic acids = nucleotides.
  • Prokaryote vs eukaryote: prokaryotes do not have a defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
  • Transport: passive = no ATP; active = requires ATP. Facilitated diffusion is also passive.
  • Osmosis: hypotonic → cell swells. Hypertonic → cell shrinks.
  • Enzymes: inhibitor at active site = competitive. Allosteric site = noncompetitive. End product inhibits first enzyme = feedback inhibition.
  • Photosynthesis: light reactions in thylakoids (produce ATP, NADPH, O₂). Calvin cycle in stroma (fixes CO₂ with Rubisco).
  • Respiration: glycolysis in cytoplasm. Pyruvate oxidation and Krebs in matrix. Chain in inner membrane. O₂ is final acceptor; ATP produced by ATP synthase.
  • Fermentation: regenerates NAD⁺. Produces no more ATP than glycolysis (only 2).

📚 Theory summary

Complete content organized by topics 4–5–6. Use it before practicing. Each subtopic includes the most common errors to avoid.

4
Topic 4. The genetic basis of life
Chromosomal organization, cell cycle, meiosis, inheritance, DNA, gene expression, and biotechnology.
T4
⭐ Key: most extensive block with highest weight. Mastering cell cycle, meiosis, Mendelian inheritance, and gene expression guarantees points.
4.1 DNA organization
  • Human DNA measures ~2 linear meters per cell; to fit in the nucleus it is compacted in levels.
  • Packaging levels: DNA → nucleosome (DNA wrapped around 8 histones) → chromatin (string of nucleosomes) → chromosome (maximum condensation, visible during division).
  • Karyotype: ordered representation of all chromosomes of a cell, grouped in pairs. Used to detect numerical or structural alterations.
  • Haploid (n): a single copy of each chromosome → gametes. Diploid (2n): two copies → somatic cells. Humans: 2n=46 (23 pairs).
  • Heterochromatin: highly condensed, transcriptionally less active (silenced genes). Euchromatin: more relaxed, active in transcription.
  • Key: the degree of compaction determines whether genes are expressed or silenced. Connects with epigenetics (4.4.8) and gene regulation (4.6).
  • Error: DNA compaction is not just structural; it controls which genes are transcribed.
4.1.1 Chromosome anatomy (technical level)
  • Sister chromatids: the two identical DNA copies resulting from replication, joined at the centromere.
  • Centromere: region of the chromosome (not an organelle) where sister chromatids remain joined until anaphase. It is constitutive heterochromatin.
  • Kinetochore: protein complex assembled on the centromere to which spindle microtubules attach. Each chromatid has its own kinetochore.
  • Telomere: chromosome end; repeated sequence (TTAGGG in vertebrates) that protects against degradation and prevents ends from fusing. Shortens with each replication.
  • Telomerase: enzyme that adds repeats to the telomere. Active in germ and stem cells; inactive in somatic cells (hence aging); reactivated in many cancers (hence "immortal").
  • Cohesin: protein complex that physically holds sister chromatids together. Cut by separase in anaphase.
  • Centriole / centrosome: organelle of the cytoplasm (not of the chromosome) from which the mitotic spindle radiates in animal cells.
  • ⚠️ Exam trap: Centriole ≠ centromere ≠ kinetochore. Centriole = cytoplasmic organelle that organizes the spindle. Centromere = chromosome region where chromatids join. Kinetochore = protein on the centromere where microtubules anchor.
  • ✏️ Fill in: Sister chromatids are held together by the protein ___ (cohesin) and separated in anaphase by the enzyme ___ (separase). Spindle microtubules anchor to the ___ (kinetochore), which sits on the ___ (centromere). Chromosome ends are called ___ (telomeres) and maintained by the enzyme ___ (telomerase).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if telomerase is mutated? Telomeres shorten with each division; when they reach a critical threshold, the cell activates apoptosis or enters senescence (cellular aging).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a cancer cell reactivates telomerase? Its telomeres don't shorten, it evades senescence, and becomes potentially "immortal" (can divide indefinitely).
4.2 Cell cycle and mitosis
  • The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of stages a cell goes through from its formation until it divides again. In eukaryotic cells it includes interphase and M phase. Its function is to allow growth, repair, tissue maintenance, and in some cases, reproduction.
  • Interphase: the longest stage of the cell cycle and not a resting phase. During it the cell is metabolically active, grows, synthesizes components, and prepares for division.
  • G1: the cell increases in size, synthesizes proteins, forms organelles, and carries out its normal functions. It also evaluates whether conditions are adequate to continue the cycle. Key: in G1 the cell has not yet duplicated its DNA.
  • S: DNA synthesis (replication) occurs. As a result, each chromosome is duplicated into two sister chromatids joined at the centromere. Key: after S phase there is more DNA, but not more independent chromosomes; each chromosome is duplicated.
  • G2: the cell continues growing, synthesizes proteins needed for division, and verifies that DNA replication was completed correctly before entering M phase.
  • Error: interphase does not mean inactivity. In G1, S, and G2, growth, synthesis, control, and preparation for division occur.
  • M phase: the cell division stage. Includes mitosis, which divides the nucleus, and cytokinesis, which divides the cytoplasm.
  • Mitosis: process by which duplicated genetic material is distributed in an orderly manner between two daughter nuclei.
  • Prophase: chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. Each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids. The mitotic spindle begins to form.
  • Prometaphase: the nuclear envelope breaks down and spindle microtubules attach to chromosomes.
  • Metaphase: chromosomes align along the equatorial plate of the cell. This alignment ensures the subsequent separation occurs correctly.
  • Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and migrate toward opposite poles of the cell. Key: in mitosis what separates are sister chromatids, not homologous chromosomes.
  • Telophase: chromosomes reach the poles, begin to decondense, and two nuclei reorganize.
  • Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm divides and two daughter cells form. Key: mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
  • Result of mitosis: two daughter cells genetically very similar to the parent cell, with the same chromosome number. Calculation: may relate to number of daughter cells, conservation of 2n, and counting chromatids/chromosomes before and after anaphase.
  • Checkpoints: checkpoints verify that the cell only advances if everything is in correct condition.
  • G1 checkpoint: checks cell size, nutrient availability, external signals, and general state before entering replication.
  • G2 checkpoint: verifies whether DNA replication was completed properly before starting mitosis.
  • Metaphase checkpoint: confirms that chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle before separation.
  • p53: the p53 protein participates in cell cycle control. If it detects significant DNA damage, it can halt the cycle, promote repair, or activate mechanisms preventing a damaged cell from continuing to divide. Key: checkpoints and p53 help prevent genetic errors and abnormal proliferation.
  • Apoptosis: programmed and regulated cell death. Eliminates damaged, unnecessary, or potentially dangerous cells; important in development, tissue renewal, and cellular balance. Error: apoptosis is not just any cell death. Must not be confused with necrosis, which typically occurs from acute, disorganized damage.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if p53 is mutated and non-functional? The cell doesn't halt the cycle despite DNA damage, doesn't repair or enter apoptosis, and can keep dividing while accumulating mutations. That is why p53 mutations appear in more than 50% of human cancers.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if the metaphase checkpoint fails? A chromatid might not be properly attached to the spindle, yet anaphase would begin → one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome and the other gets one less (aneuploidy). In meiosis this same error is called nondisjunction and causes trisomies such as Down syndrome.
4.2.3 Molecular regulation: cyclins, CDK, and APC/C
  • Cyclins: proteins whose concentration oscillates throughout the cycle. Each phase has its characteristic cyclin (G1/S cyclin, S cyclin, M cyclin).
  • CDK (cyclin-dependent kinases): enzymes that phosphorylate other proteins and control cycle progression. Inactive alone; activated when bound to a cyclin.
  • MPF (Maturation Promoting Factor): M cyclin + CDK1 complex. When activated at the end of G2, it triggers entry into mitosis.
  • APC/C (Anaphase Promoting Complex): activated in metaphase and marks securin and M cyclins for destruction.
  • Separase: enzyme that, upon release from degraded securin, cuts the cohesin holding sister chromatids together → enables anaphase.
  • 🔑 Key — anaphase cascade: active APC/C → degrades securin → releases separase → separase cuts cohesin → chromatids separate → anaphase begins.
  • ✏️ Fill in: The ___ (APC/C) complex initiates anaphase by marking ___ (securin) for destruction, releasing the enzyme ___ (separase), which cuts ___ (cohesin) that held sister chromatids together.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a mutation prevents securin from being degraded? Separase would never activate, cohesin wouldn't be cut, and chromatids wouldn't separate → cell arrested in metaphase. Similar to the mechanism of some antitumor drugs.
4.2.1 Functions of cell division
  • Enables growth and development of the multicellular organism.
  • Replaces dead or damaged cells and participates in repair and renewal of tissues.
  • In unicellular organisms, cell division functions as reproduction.
  • Essential to maintain the continuity of life in unicellular and multicellular organisms.
  • Key: not all cell division has the same purpose; mitosis is associated with growth and maintenance, meiosis with gamete formation.
4.2.2 Binary fission
  • The typical cell division mechanism of prokaryotes.
  • The circular DNA replicates and each copy attaches to different regions of the membrane.
  • The cell elongates, separates the DNA copies, and forms a septum that divides it in two.
  • Produces two daughter cells genetically very similar, unless mutations occur.
  • Error: do not confuse binary fission with mitosis; bacteria do not undergo mitosis because they have no nucleus or mitotic spindle.
4.2.6 Cell death
  • Apoptosis is a programmed, orderly, and regulated cell death.
  • Important during embryonic development, elimination of damaged cells, and maintenance of tissue balance.
  • Necrosis is typically associated with intense damage, cell rupture, and inflammation.
  • Apoptosis helps prevent problems like abnormal cell proliferation.
  • Error: apoptosis and necrosis are not synonyms; the former is controlled, the latter is usually a consequence of damage.
4.3 Meiosis
  • Meiosis is a specialized cell division that halves the chromosome number and produces haploid cells. Occurs in organisms with sexual reproduction and is fundamental for gamete formation and genetic variability.
  • Before meiosis: DNA replicates only once during S phase of interphase. ⚠️ Error: between meiosis I and meiosis II there is no new DNA replication.
  • Biological importance: allows the chromosome number of the species to remain stable after fertilization (n + n = 2n). Also generates genetic variability, which promotes diversity and adaptation in populations.
  • Meiosis I — reductional division: reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid. Homologous chromosomes separate here.
  • Prophase I: homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) and crossing over occurs. Key: the most important stage; without it there would be no recombination. Divided into 5 substages:
  • → Leptotene: chromosomes begin to condense and are visible as thin threads.
  • → Zygotene: homologous chromosomes begin pairing (synapsis) via the synaptonemal complex (protein zipper-like structure).
  • → Pachytene: synapsis is complete; crossing over occurs. Each paired homolog pair forms a tetrad or bivalent (4 chromatids).
  • → Diplotene: homologs begin to separate but remain connected at crossover points called chiasmata (visible under microscope).
  • → Diakinesis: maximum condensation; chiasmata move toward the ends and homologs are ready to align.
  • ✏️ Fill in: Synapsis begins at substage ___ (zygotene) via the ___ (synaptonemal) complex. Crossing over occurs at ___ (pachytene). The physical exchange points are called ___ (chiasmata) and are seen at substage ___ (diplotene).
  • Metaphase I: pairs of homologous chromosomes (tetrads) align at the equator. The random orientation of each pair is independent assortment.
  • Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes (one paternal, one maternal) separate and migrate to opposite poles. Sister chromatids remain joined. ⚠️ Common error: in meiosis I it is homologs that separate, NOT sister chromatids.
  • Telophase I + Interkinesis: 2 haploid cells form; each chromosome still has two sister chromatids. NO new replication occurs during interkinesis.
  • Meiosis II — equational division: does not further reduce chromosome number. Functions like mitosis but from haploid cells.
  • Anaphase II: sister chromatids separate. Key: in meiosis II chromatids DO separate (same as in mitosis).
  • Final result: 4 genetically distinct haploid cells. 3 sources of variability: ①crossing over in prophase I; ②independent assortment of homologs in metaphase I; ③random fertilization.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if there were NO crossing over? Gametes would only combine complete paternal or maternal chromosomes without mixing segments. Much less variability and reduced adaptive capacity of populations.
  • 🔬 Scenario: Separation of a homolog pair fails in anaphase I (nondisjunction) → 2 cells have an extra chromosome (n+1) and 2 have one less (n−1). If fertilized, they form a zygote with trisomy (e.g., Down syndrome) or monosomy (e.g., Turner syndrome).
  • Calculation: reduction from 2n to n, number of resulting cells (4), counting chromosomes/chromatids at each stage, comparison meiosis I vs II.
4.3.1 Sexual reproduction and variability
  • Sexual reproduction combines genetic material from two parents.
  • Meiosis and fertilization increase the genetic variability of offspring.
  • Genetic variability promotes adaptation of populations to environmental changes.
  • Crossing over and independent assortment are important sources of variation.
  • Key: genetic variability doesn't automatically mean "better," but it does mean more diversity for selection to act on.
4.3.3 Comparison of meiosis and mitosis
  • Mitosis produces 2 nearly identical diploid daughter cells; meiosis produces 4 distinct haploid cells.
  • Mitosis involves one nuclear division; meiosis involves two successive divisions.
  • In mitosis there is no synapsis or crossing over; in meiosis there is, in prophase I.
  • Mitosis conserves chromosome number (2n→2n); meiosis halves it (2n→n).
  • Key: mitosis = growth, repair, and maintenance; meiosis = sexual reproduction and genetic variability.
FeatureMitosisMeiosis IMeiosis II
Prior replicationYes (S phase)Yes (S phase)NO
Synapsis and crossing overNoYes (prophase I)No
What aligns in metaphaseIndividual chromosomesHomolog pairs (tetrads)Individual chromosomes
What separates in anaphaseSister chromatidsHomologous chromosomesSister chromatids
Result2 identical 2n cells2 n cells (chromatids still joined)4 distinct n cells
Reduces chromosomesNo (2n→2n)Yes (2n→n)No (n→n)
Main functionGrowth, repairVariability + reductionSeparate chromatids
4.3.4 Mitotic and meiotic cell divisions in the eukaryote life cycle
  • Meiosis forms haploid gametes in organisms with sexual reproduction.
  • Fertilization joins two gametes and restores the diploid number.
  • From the zygote, mitosis enables growth, development, and formation of the multicellular organism.
  • In the eukaryotic life cycle, meiosis, fertilization, and mitosis complement each other.
  • Key: meiosis reduces chromosomes; fertilization restores them; mitosis maintains chromosome number in somatic cells.
4.4.1 Physical basis of heredity: basic concepts
  • Gene: unit of hereditary information.
  • Allele: alternative version of a gene.
  • Locus: position occupied by a gene on a chromosome.
  • Genotype: genetic composition of an individual; phenotype: observable manifestation.
  • Homozygous: two identical alleles; heterozygous: two different alleles.
  • Key: do not confuse genotype with phenotype; phenotype results from genotype expression and its interaction with the environment.
4.4.1.1 Mendelian inheritance: general idea
  • Mendelian inheritance explains how certain traits are transmitted from one generation to another via alleles.
  • Based on allele segregation during gamete formation and on the combination of those alleles during fertilization.
  • Its principles work best for traits determined by a single gene with simple dominance.
  • Key: Mendelian inheritance connects the basic concepts of gene, allele, and genotype with proportions observed in offspring.
  • Error: not all heritable traits follow simple Mendelian patterns.
4.4.2 Mendel's Laws
  • Law of segregation: the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation.
  • Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes assort independently.
  • Punnett squares allow prediction of expected genotypes and phenotypes in offspring.
  • In an independent dihybrid cross, the classic F2 phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1.
  • The test cross helps infer the genotype of an individual with dominant phenotype.
  • Solved example — monohybrid cross Aa × Aa: Let A = dominant (e.g., tall stem), a = recessive (e.g., short stem). Each parent produces A and a gametes in equal proportions. Punnett square gives: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (genotypic ratio 1:2:1). In phenotype: 3 tall (AA + Aa) : 1 short (aa) → phenotypic ratio 3:1. Frequency of heterozygote Aa = 2/4 = 50%. Error: confusing 1:2:1 (genotype) with 3:1 (phenotype); they are distinct ratios.
  • Solved example — dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb: With independent assortment, 9 combinations with at least one dominant A and dominant B : 3 dominant A, homozygous b : 3 homozygous a, dominant B : 1 aabb → phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1. This ratio is an exam key.
  • Calculation: may require Punnett squares, probabilities, mono- and dihybrid ratios.
  • Error: Mendelian independence does not apply equally when there is genetic linkage.
4.4.7 Non-Mendelian patterns
  • Incomplete dominance: heterozygote with intermediate phenotype.
  • Codominance: both alleles expressed (e.g., type AB).
  • ABO: 3 alleles I^A, I^B, i → 6 genotypes.
  • Polygenic inheritance: several genes → continuous trait (height, skin color).
  • Pleiotropy: one gene → multiple phenotypic effects.
4.4.8 Epigenetics
  • Epigenetics studies heritable changes in gene expression without modifying the DNA base sequence.
  • Can involve DNA methylation and histone modifications.
  • These mechanisms activate or silence genes according to cell type, developmental stage, or environment.
  • Helps explain why cells with the same DNA can have different functions.
  • Error: epigenetics does not mean mutation; the DNA sequence can remain unchanged.
4.4.9 Genetic linkage
  • Genes located on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.
  • The closer two genes are, the less likely they are to be separated by crossing over.
  • Crossing over can break linkage and generate recombination.
  • Linkage alters expected proportions compared to Mendelian independence.
  • Calculation: may involve proportions of recombinant and non-recombinant offspring if the course requires it.
  • Error: do not assume gene independence just because two traits are being studied.
4.4.10 Sex-linked inheritance and human genetic disorders
  • Some hereditary disorders are due to gene mutations and others to chromosomal alterations.
  • Sex-linked inheritance refers to genes located on sex chromosomes, especially the X chromosome.
  • In males (XY), a recessive allele on the X chromosome is more likely to be expressed because there is no second X chromosome allele to mask it.
  • Examples of X-linked recessive traits are hemophilia and color blindness, which is why they are more frequent in males.
  • In contrast, Down, Turner, and Klinefelter syndromes are examples of chromosomal alterations, not X-linked recessive inheritance.
  • Down = trisomy 21, Turner = X0, Klinefelter = XXY.
  • Nondisjunction during meiosis can produce gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
  • Calculation: may require sex-linked crosses or family probability inference.
  • Error: do not confuse a disorder caused by a sex-linked gene mutation with a change in chromosome number.
4.5 DNA: structure and replication
  • Structure: nucleotide = phosphate group + deoxyribose + base (A, T, G, C). Antiparallel double helix. H-bond pairing: A=T (2 bonds) and G≡C (3 bonds, stronger). Chargaff's rules: %A=%T and %G=%C. Watson and Crick model (1953), diffraction data from Franklin.
  • Semiconservative replication: each daughter molecule retains one old strand + one new strand. Demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl (1958) with nitrogen isotopes.
  • Bidirectional replication: begins at replication origins (one in prokaryotes, many in eukaryotes) and proceeds in two forks in opposite directions.
  • Key enzymes (order at the fork):
  • → Helicase: opens the double helix by breaking H bonds.
  • → Topoisomerase (gyrase in prokaryotes): relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork. Many antibiotics (quinolones) target bacterial gyrase.
  • → SSB: keep single strands separated and protected.
  • → Primase: synthesizes the RNA primer (~10 nt). DNA polymerase cannot start from scratch: it needs a free 3'-OH end.
  • → DNA pol III (prok.) / Pol δ and ε (euk.): synthesizes new DNA in the 5'→3' direction, reads template strand 3'→5'. Has proofreading activity.
  • → DNA pol I: removes RNA primers and fills in gaps with DNA.
  • → DNA ligase: seals "nicks" by joining Okazaki fragments.
  • → Telomerase: extends telomeres to prevent progressive shortening of the lagging strand.
  • Leading strand (continuous): synthesized in one continuous step toward the fork. One primer.
  • Lagging strand (discontinuous): synthesized in Okazaki fragments (away from the fork) because polymerase can only synthesize 5'→3' and the template strand runs in the opposite direction.
  • ✏️ Fill in: The enzyme ___ (helicase) opens the double helix. ___ (Topoisomerase) relieves supercoiling. ___ (SSB) proteins prevent strand reannealing. ___ (Primase) synthesizes the primer. DNA polymerase synthesizes in the ___ (5'→3') direction. On the lagging strand, ___ (Okazaki) fragments form and are joined by ___ (DNA ligase). ___ (Telomerase) extends telomeres.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if topoisomerase fails? DNA ahead of the fork would accumulate so much supercoiling tension that helicase couldn't advance and replication would stop. (Application: antibiotics like ciprofloxacin inhibit bacterial gyrase.)
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why is the lagging strand synthesized in Okazaki fragments? Because DNA polymerase can only synthesize 5'→3', and the lagging template strand runs in the direction opposite to fork movement; so it is synthesized in short fragments "backward."
  • ⚠️ Error: DNA polymerase NEVER synthesizes 3'→5'. It only adds nucleotides to the 3'-OH end. That's why a primer is needed and why the lagging strand exists.
Enzyme / proteinFunction
HelicaseBreaks hydrogen bonds and opens the double helix
Topoisomerase (gyrase)Relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork. Target of quinolone antibiotics
SSBKeeps single strands separated and protected from nucleases
PrimaseSynthesizes the RNA primer (~10 nt); DNA pol cannot start from scratch
DNA polymerase III / Pol δ and εSynthesizes new DNA in the 5'→3' direction; has proofreading activity
DNA polymerase IRemoves RNA primers and fills in gaps with DNA

4.5.1 DNA as genetic material
  • DNA stores hereditary information in most organisms.
  • Its stable structure and capacity for replication allow information to be transmitted from one generation to the next.
  • Genes are DNA segments containing functional information.
  • DNA directs RNA and protein synthesis through gene expression.
  • Key: DNA as genetic material implies storage, transmission, and expression of information.
4.5.4 Mutations
  • Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence. Origin: spontaneous (replication errors) or induced (UV radiation, X-rays, chemical mutagens).
  • Gene mutations by mechanism — substitution: one base is replaced by another. Transition: purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (A↔G, C↔T). Transversion: purine↔pyrimidine (A↔C, G↔T).
  • Insertion: one or more bases are added → shifts the reading frame. Gene deletion: one or more bases are lost → also shifts the reading frame.
  • Gene mutations by effect on the protein:
  • → Silent: changes the codon but does NOT change the amino acid (thanks to code degeneracy). Usually occur at the 3rd base of the codon.
  • → Missense: changes the codon AND changes the amino acid. Classic example: GAG→GUG in β-globin changes glutamic acid to valine → sickle cell anemia.
  • → Nonsense: introduces a premature stop codon → truncated protein, generally non-functional.
  • → Frameshift: insertion or deletion of bases (not a multiple of 3) that shifts the reading frame → changes all codons after the mutation point → completely different protein from that point on.
  • Structural chromosomal mutations: Deletion: loss of a fragment (e.g., Cri-du-chat syndrome from deletion of the short arm of chr. 5). Duplication: fragment appears twice. Inversion: fragment is reversed. Translocation: fragment moves to another chromosome (e.g., 9-22 translocation → Philadelphia chromosome → chronic myeloid leukemia).
  • ✏️ Fill in: Loss of a chromosomal fragment is called ___ (deletion), its doubling is ___ (duplication), reversal is ___ (inversion), and movement to another chromosome is ___ (translocation). A substitution that doesn't change the amino acid is ___ (silent). One that introduces a premature stop codon is ___ (nonsense). An insertion/deletion that shifts the reading frame is ___ (frameshift).
  • Key: mutation is the original source of new alleles. Without mutation there is no variation; without variation there is no evolution.
  • ⚠️ Error: mutation does not always mean serious disease. A silent mutation doesn't change the protein. The effect depends on the type of change and its context.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a mutation introduces a stop codon in the middle of a gene? Translation terminates early → truncated protein, generally non-functional (nonsense mutation). Can cause serious disease if the protein is essential.
4.6 Gene expression and regulation
  • DNA → mRNA (transcription, in nucleus) → protein (translation, ribosome).
  • AUG = start; UAA/UAG/UGA = stop. Codon = triplet in mRNA.
  • Eukaryotes: introns removed, exons joined; poly-A tail and 5' cap.
  • lac operon = regulation in prokaryotes.
4.6.1 Genetic code
  • The genetic code relates mRNA codons to specific amino acids.
  • It is nearly universal, degenerate, and unambiguous.
  • Degenerate: different codons can encode the same amino acid.
  • Unambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid or signal.
  • Error: codon is not the same as gene; a codon is a triplet, not a complete protein.
4.6.2 Transcription
  • Transcription copies information from DNA to an RNA molecule. In eukaryotes it occurs in the nucleus.
  • Eukaryotic RNA polymerases: RNA Pol I transcribes ribosomal RNA. RNA Pol II transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes). RNA Pol III transcribes tRNA and small RNAs.
  • TATA box: promoter sequence located ~25–30 nt before the transcription start site. Serves as anchor point for transcription factors that recruit RNA Pol II.
  • Transcription factors: proteins that bind to the promoter and help (or prevent) transcription of specific genes. They are the basis of differential gene regulation.
  • Pre-mRNA processing in eukaryotes: ①Addition of 5' cap (7-methylguanosine, protects against degradation and facilitates translation start). ②3' polyadenylation (poly-A tail, ~200 A, stabilizes mRNA). ③Splicing: removal of introns and joining of exons by the spliceosome.
  • Alternative splicing: exons from the same pre-mRNA can be combined in different ways → one gene can produce several different proteins.
  • ⚠️ Error: do not confuse template strand (3'→5', read by polymerase) with coding strand (5'→3', same sequence as mRNA with U instead of T).
  • ✏️ Fill in: The RNA pol that transcribes protein-coding genes is ___ (RNA Pol II). The site where it binds to the promoter is called ___ (TATA box). The process that removes introns is called ___ (splicing), carried out by the ___ (spliceosome) complex. Protection of the 5' end of mRNA is called ___ (5' cap).
4.6.3 Translation (expanded)
  • RNA types: mRNA (carries the message), tRNA (transports amino acids, recognizes codons with its anticodon), rRNA (structural and catalytic component of the ribosome — it is a ribozyme).
  • Ribosome in prokaryotes: 30S + 50S = 70S. In eukaryotes: 40S + 60S = 80S.
  • Ribosome sites: A site (aminoacyl: incoming charged tRNA). P site (peptidyl: where the growing chain is and peptide bond forms). E site (exit: empty tRNA leaves).
  • Initiation: in prokaryotes, the small subunit recognizes the Shine-Dalgarno sequence near the AUG. In eukaryotes, it recognizes the 5' cap and scans to the AUG in Kozak context.
  • Elongation: aminoacyl-tRNA enters A site → peptidyl transferase catalyzes peptide bond → translocation: ribosome advances one codon → tRNA moves A→P→E.
  • Termination: a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) reaches the A site → release factors enter → protein is released.
  • Polysomes: several ribosomes simultaneously translate the same mRNA → greater protein production.
  • ✏️ Fill in: The incoming tRNA arrives at site ___ (A). The peptide bond forms at site ___ (P). The empty tRNA exits through site ___ (E). In prokaryotes, initiation depends on the ___ (Shine-Dalgarno) sequence. In eukaryotes, the ___ (5' cap) and ___ (Kozak) sequence. Stop codons are ___ (UAA, UAG, UGA).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a mutation changes the anticodon of a tRNA? That tRNA will carry its amino acid to the wrong codon → many proteins will have a changed amino acid at specific positions. Can be lethal.
4.6.4.1 Gene regulation in prokaryotes: lac operon
  • Prokaryotes regulate related genes by grouping them in operons. The E. coli lac operon (Jacob and Monod, 1961) is the classic model.
  • Components: Regulatory gene lacI (encodes the repressor); Promoter (Plac, where RNA polymerase binds); Operator (O, repressor binding site); Structural genes: lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase).
  • Negative regulation — the repressor: without lactose, the repressor binds to the operator and blocks transcription. With lactose (allolactose acts as inducer), the repressor detaches from the operator → genes are transcribed.
  • Positive regulation — CAP/CRP: with low glucose (high cAMP), the CAP (CRP) protein binds the promoter and increases RNA polymerase affinity → more transcription. With high glucose, CAP doesn't act even if lactose is present.
  • 4 key scenarios (exam questions):
  • ①No glucose + lactose → genes active (maximum transcription: repressor off + CAP on).
  • ②Glucose + lactose → genes transcribe but little (repressor off but CAP inactive).
  • ③No glucose + no lactose → genes blocked (repressor on).
  • ④Glucose + no lactose → genes blocked (repressor on + CAP inactive).
  • ✏️ Fill in: The gene encoding the lac operon repressor is ___ (lacI). The repressor binds to the ___ (operator). The molecule acting as inducer is ___ (allolactose). The positive regulatory protein is ___ (CAP/CRP). When glucose is low, the level of ___ (cAMP) increases.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if the lac operon operator has a mutation and the repressor can't bind? The genes lacZ, lacY, and lacA would be transcribed constitutively (always active), even without lactose present. This wastes cellular resources.
4.6.4.2 Gene regulation in eukaryotes
  • Eukaryotic gene regulation can occur at multiple levels:
  • ①Chromatin: chromatin packaging (heterochromatin vs euchromatin) and histone modifications (acetylation activates, methylation can silence).
  • ②Transcription: transcription factors can activate or inhibit specific genes; enhancers can be far from the promoter.
  • ③RNA processing: alternative splicing allows different proteins from the same gene.
  • ④Translation: miRNA (microRNA) block translation or induce mRNA degradation.
  • ⑤Post-translational: ubiquitination marks proteins for degradation in the proteasome; phosphorylation activates/inactivates proteins.
  • Key: different cells have the same DNA but express different genes. Differential regulation explains cell specialization (how a neuron and a muscle cell are so different with the same genome).
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why can two cells with the same DNA be so different? Because they differentially regulate which genes are expressed. Transcription factors, chromatin structure, and miRNAs determine the expression profile of each cell type.
4.7 DNA technology
  • PCR amplifies specific sequences from minimal amounts.
  • Recombinant DNA: cut (endonucleases) + insert into vector → host cell.
  • GMOs, gene therapy, sequencing, genomics → medical and agricultural applications.
  • Bioethics: risks, access, and responsible use.
4.8 Biotechnology
  • Definition: biotechnology is the use of organisms, cells, or biological molecules to produce food, medicines, and other goods.
  • Traditional biotechnology: use of yeasts to make bread, beer, and wine; selective breeding of plants; selective breeding of animals.
  • Modern biotechnology: employs genetic engineering; refers to more direct methods of altering DNA; genes can be deleted, added, or changed.
  • Key definition: recombinant DNA = DNA containing genes or parts of genes from two or more organisms. Modern biotechnology uses recombinant DNA.
  • Restriction enzymes and ligases: restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; ligases join DNA fragments. Some restriction enzymes generate "sticky ends" (single-stranded cohesive ends) that facilitate joining with other fragments.
  • Recombinant DNA in nature: sexual reproduction recombines DNA; in meiosis I homologous chromosomes exchange DNA (crossing over); bacteria can take up DNA from the environment by transformation; some viruses can transfer DNA between species.
  • Key definition: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is a technique that amplifies a segment of DNA. It can produce billions of copies of selected DNA fragments. Applications: forensics, cloning, production of transgenic organisms, diagnosis, analysis of DNA from crime scenes.
  • Gel electrophoresis: technique to separate DNA segments by size by applying an electric field to a gel.
  • STR (Short Tandem Repeats): short repeated sequences scattered throughout the genome; used to identify individuals with high precision in forensic laboratories.
  • DNA probes: used in hybridization techniques to label specific nucleotide sequences (detect presence of a gene or target sequence).
  • CRISPR-Cas9: modern tool enabling precise DNA editing (cutting and modifying genes at a specific site).
  • Key definition: a GMO (genetically modified organism) is a plant, animal, or microorganism whose DNA has been modified through genetic engineering.
  • Steps to create a GMO: 1) obtain the desired gene, 2) clone the gene, 3) insert the gene into host organism cells.
  • Obtaining the desired gene: DNA can be isolated from cells; cut with restriction enzymes; separated by gel electrophoresis; or synthesized chemically.
  • Molecular cloning: consists of inserting a gene into a bacterial plasmid; that plasmid replicates when the bacterium divides → many copies of the gene are obtained.
  • Gene insertion into host: bacteria or viruses as vectors; biolistics or "gene gun"; chemical transfection; injection of foreign DNA into fertilized eggs.
  • Examples of transgenic organisms: modified corn, cotton, and soy; crops resistant to insects or herbicides; Bt cotton plants (insecticidal toxin); animals modified to produce more wool, more protein in milk, or less fat.
  • Genomics: study of an organism's complete genome (structure, function, and evolution of genes).
  • Human Genome Project: the human genome contains approximately 20,000 genes; those genes comprise approximately 2% of DNA; much of the rest is non-coding DNA.
  • Medical impact: understanding the genome has great impact in medicine; many human diseases are caused by defective alleles; PCR is a diagnostic tool; DNA probes are also used.
  • Key definition: gene therapy is the attempt to cure diseases by inserting, deleting, or altering genes in a patient's cells.
  • Common error: PCR amplifies DNA, it does not modify it.
  • Common error: molecular cloning (copying a gene into a plasmid) is NOT the same as cloning a whole organism.
  • Common error: "recombinant DNA" does not mean any spontaneous mutation; it implies combining DNA from two or more organisms in the laboratory (or through specific biological processes such as transformation or viruses).
  • Applications by area: medicine (PCR/probe diagnosis, gene therapy, human insulin production in bacteria), forensics (STR analysis, crime scenes, paternity testing), agriculture (pest/herbicide-resistant crops, higher yield, better nutritional value).
