Topic 5. Evolution of Life
Evolutionary thought, population genetics, Hardy-Weinberg, selection, speciation.
T5
5.1 Principles of Evolution
  • Definition: evolution is the change that occurs over time in the characteristics of populations.
  • Ancient preceding idea: early biological studies did not include the concept of evolution; it was believed that all organisms were created simultaneously and that species remained unchanged.
  • Naturalists' observations: the diversity of life was greater than thought; each region had its own set of species; some local species closely resembled each other; fossils of now-extinct organisms were discovered. These observations clashed with the idea of immutable species.
  • Lamarck: proposed a mechanism of evolution based on inheritance of acquired characteristics: the use and disuse of structures modifies them during an individual's lifetime, and those modifications are passed on to offspring. Important: Lamarck proposed an evolutionary mechanism, but did NOT propose natural selection.
  • Darwin: traveled on the ship Beagle; observed species in many habitats; arrived at the Galápagos in 1835.
  • Galápagos finches: Darwin observed several species of finches with different beaks, each associated with a type of food (hard seeds, insects, nectar, etc.). Beak size and shape are related to efficient exploitation of available food resources.
  • Darwin and Wallace: the theory of evolution by natural selection was presented by Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace in 1858.
  • Four postulates of Darwin and Wallace:
    1. Individuals vary within a population.
    2. Traits are inherited from parents to offspring.
    3. Some individuals do not survive or reproduce.
    4. Survival and reproduction are not determined by chance.
  • Postulate 1 — Individual variation: each individual has a unique combination of traits; differences exist in size, color, environmental tolerance, resistance to parasites or infections; variation extends down to the level of DNA.
  • Postulate 2 — Inheritance: variation is heritable; Mendel showed that traits can be transmitted to offspring through hereditary factors (genes).
  • Postulate 3 — Overproduction: each species can produce more offspring than survive; populations tend to remain relatively stable; overproduction exists: more organisms must be born than survive to reproduce.
  • Postulate 4 — Non-random reproductive success: reproductive success depends on an individual's traits; those with favorable combinations survive longer and leave more offspring. Class examples: larger elephant seals dominate harems and leave more offspring; snapdragon plants with flowers that better attract pollinators; antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive treatment and proliferate.
  • Natural selection: process by which nature "selects" individuals with advantageous traits; they survive longer and leave more offspring, thus modifying populations over time.
  • Key idea: an individual does NOT evolve; a population DOES. An individual is born with its genotype and dies with it; what changes over time are the frequencies of traits within the population.
  • Evidence of evolution: evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biochemistry, and genetics.
  • Fossils: show progressive series; new species arise from previous species. Example: evolution of whales from terrestrial limbed ancestors, through semi-aquatic forms, to today's fully aquatic whales.
  • Comparative anatomy: comparison of the bodies of different organisms; similarities are explained by common ancestry; body structures modified for different functions.
  • Homologous structures: structures with the same evolutionary origin, even if they may have different functions (e.g., human arm, bat wing, whale flipper → same bone plan).
  • Vestigial structures: inherited structures that appear to have no defined purpose or have reduced function. Examples: remnants of hind limbs in whales and boa constrictors (reduced hip and femur bones with no locomotor function).
  • Convergent evolution: natural selection can cause non-homologous structures with similar functions to become very similar.
  • Analogous structures: structures that are similar externally or functionally, but with different evolutionary origins (e.g., insect wing and bird wing: same function, different origin).
  • Embryology: vertebrate embryos show remarkable similarity in their early stages (pharyngeal arches, tail, segmentation), evidencing common ancestry.
  • Biochemical and genetic evidence: molecular similarity between species; existence of homologous molecules; similarities in DNA sequences (the closer the relationship, the greater the similarity).
  • Universal biochemical similarities: all cells use DNA, RNA, ribosomes, nearly the same genetic code, approximately the same 20 amino acids, and ATP as energy carrier → strong evidence of common origin.
  • Artificial selection: observable evidence that populations can change through selective breeding in domestic plants and animals (dog breeds, corn varieties, dairy cattle) → demonstrates that selection generates change in just a few generations.
  • Common error: Lamarck did NOT propose natural selection (that was Darwin and Wallace).
  • Common error: homologous and analogous structures are NOT the same thing. Homologous = same origin; analogous = same function but different origin.
  • Common error: evolution does NOT occur because an organism "wants to change" or "needs to." Variations exist randomly; selection acts on what already exists.
  • Common error: do NOT confuse evolution of the individual with evolution of the population. Only populations evolve.
5.1.1 History of Evolutionary Thought and Darwin
  • In ancient views, the idea of fixed and immutable species predominated.
  • Lamarck proposed an evolutionary mechanism based on use and disuse and inheritance of acquired traits.
  • Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection as the principal mechanism of evolutionary change.
  • Darwin gathered observations from biogeography, fossils, and variation in organisms, including the Galápagos finches.
  • Error: Lamarck did not propose natural selection.
5.1.2 Synthetic Theory of Evolution
  • The synthetic theory integrates Mendelian genetics, mutation, recombination, natural selection, and population evolution.
  • Evolution is understood as change in allele frequencies over time.
  • It unites hereditary mechanisms with the evolutionary change observed in populations.
  • Key: the synthetic theory connects genetics and evolution.
5.1.3 Evidence of Evolution
  • Evolution is supported by fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography, biochemistry, and genetics.
  • Homologous structures indicate common ancestry; analogous structures reflect convergent evolution.
  • Vestigial structures support the idea of evolutionary change.
  • Molecular similarities between species reflect evolutionary relationships.
  • Error: homologous and analogous are not equivalent.
5.2.1 Population Genetics
  • Studies the distribution of alleles and genotypes in a population.
  • Evolution, at this level, consists of changes in allele frequencies over time.
  • The set of alleles in a population constitutes its gene pool.
  • Mutation, selection, genetic drift, and gene flow can modify that pool.
  • Key: population evolution = change in allele frequencies, not individual change.
  • Calculation: may require interpreting allele and genotypic frequencies.
5.2.2 Hardy-Weinberg
  • p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Heterozygotes = 2pq.
  • 5 conditions: no mutation, no selection, random mating, no migration, large population size.
  • Key: if the population deviates from equilibrium → evolution is acting.
  • Describes the expected genetic equilibrium in an ideal population.
  • If p is the frequency of one allele and q the other, then p + q = 1.
  • Expected genotypic frequencies are p², 2pq, and q².
  • If a population deviates from equilibrium, some evolutionary factor is acting.
  • Step-by-step solved example: Suppose the frequency of allele a in a population is q = 0.3.
    Step 1 — Find p: p = 1 − q = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.
    Step 2 — Calculate genotypic frequencies:
       • Homozygous dominant AA = p² = 0.7² = 0.49 (49%).
       • Heterozygotes Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42 (42%).
       • Homozygous recessive aa = q² = 0.3² = 0.09 (9%).
    Step 3 — Verification: 0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1.00 ✓.
    Step 4 — Interpretation: if in the real population 12% are aa instead of the expected 9%, the frequency of q is increasing → some evolutionary force is acting. Common error: forgetting that aa = q² (not q). To find q from the frequency of recessive aa, take the square root: q = √(frequency of aa).
  • Calculation: may require finding p, q, p², 2pq, q², frequency of heterozygotes or carriers.
5.2.3 Adaptive Changes in Allele Frequencies
  • If an allele improves survival or reproduction, it can increase in frequency in the population.
  • Natural selection favors advantageous heritable combinations in a specific environment.
  • When the environment changes, which traits are favorable may also change.
  • Adaptations arise through selection on existing variation, not through the organism's conscious need.
  • Error: adaptive does not mean "wanted" or "sought" by the organism.
5.2.4–5 Evolutionary Forces and Types of Selection
  • Mutation is the original source of new alleles; without it there is no heritable variation.
  • Genetic drift produces random changes in allele frequencies, especially strong in small populations. Cases: founder effect (few individuals form a new population) and bottleneck (drastic population reduction).
  • Gene flow occurs when individuals or gametes move between populations → homogenizes allele frequencies and introduces new alleles.
  • Inbreeding and non-random mating change genotypic frequencies (more homozygotes) but not necessarily allele frequencies.
  • Key: not all evolutionary changes are due to natural selection. Drift, gene flow, and mutation also alter the gene pool.
ForceMechanismEffect on gene pool
MutationChanges in the DNA sequenceCreates new alleles (original source)
Natural selectionDifferential survival/reproductionIncreases advantageous alleles (non-random)
Genetic driftRandom sampling of gametesChanges frequencies randomly; strong when N is small
Gene flowMigration of individuals or gametesHomogenizes populations; introduces new alleles
Non-random matingMate choice, inbreedingChanges genotypic frequencies, not allelic; increases homozygosity
Type of selectionWhat it favorsExample
StabilizingThe average phenotype; eliminates extremes; distribution narrowsHuman birth weight (very low or very high → lower survival)
DirectionalOne extreme of the range; shifts the distribution meanPeppered moth during Industrial Revolution; finch beaks after drought
DisruptiveBoth extremes; average phenotype is at a disadvantage; bimodal distributionFinches with very large or very small beaks when only extreme-sized seeds exist
5.2.6 Sexual Selection
  • Favors traits that increase mating success, even if they don't always improve survival.
  • Can act through competition between same-sex individuals or through mate choice.
  • Explains ornaments, courtship behaviors, and sexual dimorphism in many species.
  • Key: evolutionary success also depends on leaving offspring.
5.2.7 Artificial Selection
  • Occurs when humans choose which individuals reproduce based on desired traits.
  • Has produced domestic breeds and agricultural varieties with very marked characteristics.
  • Shows that a population can change in just a few generations if reproduction is not random.
  • Error: artificial selection is not the same as natural selection; the selective agent changes.
5.3.1 Biological Species Concept
  • According to the biological concept, a species is a set of populations whose individuals can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
  • Reproductive isolation helps keep species separate.
  • This concept works best in organisms with sexual reproduction.
  • Error: physical resemblance alone is not enough to belong to the same species.
5.3 Speciation
  • Prezygotic reproductive isolation (prevents fertilization): Ecological (different habitats), Temporal (different breeding seasons), Behavioral (different courtships), Mechanical (anatomical incompatibility), Gametic (gametes don't recognize each other).
  • Postzygotic reproductive isolation (fertilization occurs but offspring fail): Zygote or embryo inviability; Hybrid sterility (classic example: the mule, horse × donkey cross, is viable but sterile); Loss of fertility in subsequent generations.
  • Types of speciation by geography:
  • → Allopatric: geographic separation by a physical barrier (river, mountain, glacier). The most common. Each subpopulation accumulates different mutations and experiences different selective pressures.
  • → Sympatric: in the same geographic space, without a barrier. Mechanisms: ecological divergence, assortative mating, and especially polyploidy in plants.
  • → Parapatric: adjacent areas with limited gene flow at the contact zone. Divergent selection in each habitat.
  • → Peripatric: special case of allopatric where a small population becomes isolated at the periphery → strong genetic drift (founder effect).
  • Polyploidy as instantaneous sympatric speciation: Autopolyploidy = chromosome set duplication within a single species. Allopolyploidy = hybridization between two species + chromosome duplication. Example: modern wheat (Triticum aestivum, hexaploid 6n) arose through hybridization and polyploidization.
  • Key: a polyploid crossed with the original species produces 3n offspring → sterile (meiosis with odd chromosomes impossible) → instantaneous reproductive isolation.
  • Anagenesis = linear transformation of one species into another. Cladogenesis = one species splits into two (branching) → mechanism that increases biodiversity.
  • ✏️ Fill in: Speciation with a geographic barrier is ___ (allopatric). Without a barrier, in the same space, ___ (sympatric). The chromosomal duplication that produces instant speciation is ___ (polyploidy). The branching of one species into two is ___ (cladogenesis). A polyploid crossed with the diploid species produces ___ offspring (3n, sterile).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a lizard population were divided by a new river? Each subpopulation accumulates different mutations and faces different selective pressures. After thousands of generations, if they come back into contact they may no longer interbreed → complete allopatric speciation.
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why does polyploidy produce nearly instantaneous reproductive isolation? Because crossing a polyploid (4n) with the original species (2n) produces 3n offspring, which cannot perform meiosis correctly (odd chromosomes without a partner) → sterile hybrids. Polyploids only reproduce among themselves.
5.3.4 Macroevolution, Extinction, and Evolutionary Rate
  • Macroevolution analyzes evolutionary patterns at the species level or above (genera, families, classes).
  • Includes the origin of major groups, adaptive radiations (rapid diversification upon reaching a new environment or after extinction), and long-term changes in biodiversity.
  • Extinction eliminates lineages and modifies evolutionary history. Mass extinctions can open niches for new radiations. Example: extinction of non-avian dinosaurs 66 Ma ago paved the way for the mammalian radiation.
  • Gradualism (Darwin): slow and continuous change over time.
  • Punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould): long periods of stability (stasis) interrupted by rapid evolutionary changes associated with speciation.
  • Key: accumulated microevolutionary processes (changes in allele frequencies) contribute to macroevolutionary patterns (origin of new species and clades).
6
Topic 6. Biological Diversity
Origin of life and first cells (6.1). Topics 6.2–6.4 belong to Exam Unit 3.
T6
6.1 Origin of Life
  • Miller-Urey: abiotic synthesis of amino acids under primitive conditions (no O₂).
  • Chemical evolution: simple compounds → macromolecules → protocells.
  • First cells: anaerobic heterotrophic prokaryotes.
  • Cyanobacteria → O₂ into the atmosphere. Endosymbiosis → mitochondria and chloroplasts.
6.1.1 Main Stages: Planet Formation
  • Primitive Earth formed billions of years ago under conditions very different from today.
  • It had intense volcanic activity, high temperatures, intense radiation, and frequent electrical storms.
  • The primitive atmosphere had a different composition and virtually no free oxygen.
  • These conditions inform hypotheses about chemical evolution and the origin of life.
  • Key: the origin of life is studied within the physicochemical context of the primitive planet.
6.1.2 Theories on the Origin of Life
  • Modern abiogenesis proposes that life arose from non-living matter through gradual physicochemical processes.
  • Oparin and Haldane suggested that simple molecules could give rise to more complex organic compounds.
  • Other proposals explore environments such as hydrothermal vents and prebiotic synthesis in various scenarios.
  • These theories aim to explain the origin of biological systems from natural processes.
  • Error: a theory on the origin of life does not mean that the complete formation of a cell has already been observed in a laboratory.
6.1.3 Formation of Macromolecules, Protocells, and First Cells
  • Simple organic molecules could give rise to macromolecules with increasingly complex functions.
  • Protocells would have been aggregates with rudimentary membranes and some internal chemical organization.
  • The first cells were likely prokaryotes, anaerobic, and heterotrophic.
  • Later, photosynthetic organisms appeared that contributed to increasing atmospheric oxygen.
  • Key: a protocell is not equivalent to a complete modern cell; it represents a preceding stage.

BottleneckDrastic reduction in population size; intensifies genetic drift
DeletionLoss of a DNA or chromosomal fragment
Genetic driftRandom change in allele frequencies; especially strong when N is small
Diploid (2n)Two copies of each chromosome (somatic cells; humans: 2n=46)

📚 Theory Summary — Exam Unit 3

Organization of information on species, biological diversity (viruses, prions, prokaryotes, protists, plants, fungi, invertebrate animals, and chordates) and ecology (populations, communities, ecosystems, and biosphere). Identical structure to U1/U2: collapsible sections by subtopic, with key ideas and common errors highlighted.

6
Topic 6 — Organization of Information on Species and Biological Diversity
Systematics, taxonomy, viruses/prions, prokaryotes, protists, plants, fungi, invertebrate animals, and chordates
Summary
6.2 Systematics, Taxonomy, and the Tree of Life (6.2.1 – 6.2.4)
  • 6.2.1 Systematic biology: integrates classification + phylogeny + diversity. It is not just "naming things" — that is taxonomy.
  • Taxon: any group recognized in the hierarchy (species, genus, family, domain).
  • Clade: common ancestor + ALL its descendants (monophyletic group). If a descendant is excluded, it is not a valid clade.
  • 6.2.2.1 Linnaeus hierarchy (8 levels): Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. Higher = broader and more diverse; lower = more specific.
  • 6.2.2.2 Binomial system: Genus (capitalized) + specific epithet (lowercase), in italics. E.g.: Homo sapiens, Escherichia coli.
  • 6.2.3 Tools: comparative anatomy, embryology, fossil record, molecular evidence (DNA/RNA). Ribosomal RNA → basis of the three-domain system.
  • Homology vs. Analogy: homology = same origin, different function (e.g., bat wing and human arm); analogy = same function, different origin (e.g., insect wing and bird wing).
  • 6.2.3.1 Phylogenetic trees: node = hypothetical ancestor; branch = diverging lineage; root = oldest ancestor. Visual position (top/bottom) does NOT indicate "more evolved".
  • 6.2.4 Carl Woese (1977): 16S ribosomal RNA → discovered that prokaryotes are not a homogeneous group → three domains: Bacteria + Archaea + Eukarya.
Concept What it does Question it answers
TaxonomyNames and classifies"What is it called and where do I place it?"
PhylogeneticsReconstructs evolutionary relationships"Where does it come from and who is it related to?"
SystematicsIntegrates both within the study of diversity"How is all this diversity organized evolutionarily?"
Trait Bacteria Archaea Eukarya
True nucleusNoNoYes
Cell wallWith peptidoglycanNo peptidoglycan (pseudopeptidoglycan)Variable or absent
Membrane lipidsEster-linkedEther-linked (unique in life)Ester-linked
Bacterial antibioticsYes (sensitive)No (resistant)No
Histones on DNANoYes (similar to eukaryotes)Yes
⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Systematics ≠ taxonomy ≠ phylogenetics — not interchangeable. (2) "Reptilia" without birds is NOT a clade (paraphyletic). (3) Position on a phylogenetic tree does not mean "more evolved." (4) Archaea is NOT a type of bacteria. (5) "homo Sapiens" is incorrect — must be Homo sapiens.
🔬 Scenario: Unicellular organism with no nucleus, no peptidoglycan, ether-linked lipids, lives at 90°C. Bacteria or Archaea? A: Archaea. No-peptidoglycan + ether lipids are diagnostic for Archaea, not Bacteria.
🔬 Phylogenetic tree scenario: A and B share a node; that node connects to C at an older node. Who is most closely related? A: A and B to each other — they share a more recent common ancestor than either does with C.
6.3.1 Virus Structure and Characteristics — Lytic and Lysogenic Cycles
  • Viruses are acellular entities: genetic material (DNA or RNA, never both) + protein capsid. Some have a host-membrane envelope.
  • They are not cells: no cytoplasm, ribosomes, or own metabolism → obligate intracellular parasites. They infect all domains; those infecting bacteria = bacteriophages.
  • Lytic cycle: replicates immediately → lysis → cell dies → releases hundreds of new viruses.
  • Lysogenic cycle: viral genome integrates into the host chromosome as a prophage → cell survives and divides normally for many generations → stress (UV) can induce the prophage to enter the lytic cycle.
Feature Lytic cycle Lysogenic cycle
Replicates immediately?YesNo (remains integrated)
State of viral genomeActive, replicatingIntegrated as prophage
Does the cell die?Yes, by lysisNot immediately; can survive for generations
Produces viral particles?Yes, hundredsNo, until activated
Lysogenic → lytic trigger—Cell stress (UV radiation, chemicals)
🔬 Step-by-step process: Lytic cycle (5 stages)

1. Adsorption: the virus recognizes specific receptors on the host surface and attaches. 2. Penetration: the viral genetic material enters the cell (in phages, the capsid stays outside). 3. Biosynthesis: the viral genome hijacks the cell machinery to replicate and produce viral proteins. 4. Assembly (maturation): the genome is packaged into newly synthesized capsids. 5. Release by lysis: viral enzymes break the cell wall, the cell bursts and releases viral particles into the environment.

⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Not every virus destroys the cell immediately — in the lysogenic cycle it can remain inactive for generations. (2) Virus ≠ small cell. (3) Viruses do not belong to any classical biological kingdom (they are acellular).
🔬 Scenario: A bacterium with an integrated prophage is exposed to UV radiation. What do you predict? A: The prophage activates → lysogenic→lytic transition → actively replicates → lyses the bacterium.
6.3.2 Viroids and Prions — Non-cellular Infectious Agents
Agent Composition Coat Typical host
VirusNucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + proteinYes (capsid)All domains
ViroidShort, circular, naked RNANoPlants (crops)
PrionMisfolded protein (no nucleic acid)NoAnimals (neurodegenerative diseases)

The prion is revolutionary: it transmits "information" through the protein conformation, without nucleic acid. Examples: "mad cow disease" (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

⚠️ Exam trap: Viroids and prions are NOT types of viruses. They are agents with completely different chemical natures.
🔬 Scenario: Infectious agent resistant to nucleases (which destroy nucleic acid) but sensitive to proteases. What type is it? A: Prion — its nature is exclusively protein-based.
6.3.3–6.3.6 Prokaryotes: Structure, Bacteria, Archaea, and Reproduction
  • Prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Circular DNA in the nucleoid, 70S ribosomes. "Prokaryote" ≠ "bacterium" (Archaea is also prokaryote).
  • Bacteria: cell wall with peptidoglycan. Classified by shape (cocci, bacilli, spirilla), Gram staining (+/−), and metabolism.
  • Gram-positive (purple): thick peptidoglycan wall retains crystal violet. Gram-negative (pink): thin wall + outer membrane with lipopolysaccharides (LPS = endotoxins) → alcohol washes out crystal violet.
  • Special structures: flagella (locomotion), biofilms (attached communities), endospores (extreme resistance — not reproduction).
  • Archaea: no peptidoglycan (pseudopeptidoglycan), ether-linked lipids, complex RNA polymerase. Not all are extremophiles. More closely related to Eukarya than to Bacteria in molecular phylogeny.
  • Reproduction: binary fission (asexual). E. coli divides every 20 min under optimal conditions.
HGT mechanism How it works Vehicle
TransformationBacterium takes up free DNA from the environment (from dead bacteria)Free DNA
TransductionBacteriophage accidentally transports bacterial DNA from one cell to anotherVirus (phage)
ConjugationDonor cell transfers a plasmid to a recipient via a sex pilus (direct contact)Pilus / plasmid
🔬 Step-by-step process: Bacterial conjugation

1. Donor bacterium extends sex pilus toward recipient. 2. Pilus retracts → direct contact → cytoplasmic bridge. 3. Donor's plasmid is nicked and one strand is transferred via rolling-circle. 4. In the recipient, the complementary strand is synthesized and the plasmid re-circularizes. 5. Both cells now carry the plasmid. If it carries resistance genes → both are resistant. Conjugation allows resistance to spread between different species, explaining the speed of propagation.

⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Conjugation is NOT "bacterial sex" (no gamete fusion or meiosis). (2) Bacterial conjugation ≠ Paramecium conjugation. (3) Archaea is NOT a subclass of Bacteria. (4) Not all archaea are extremophiles. (5) Endospore = resistance, NOT reproduction.
🔬 Scenario: A Gram-positive bacterium loses the ability to synthesize peptidoglycan by mutation. What happens? A: It loses osmotic support → lyses easily. It stops retaining crystal violet (no longer Gram+). Unaffected by penicillin (which inhibits peptidoglycan synthesis). Mechanism analogous to penicillin's action.
🔬 Conjugation scenario: An ampicillin-sensitive bacterium is mixed with a resistant one carrying the resistance gene on a plasmid. After some time, the formerly sensitive ones are also resistant. What happened? A: Conjugation: the plasmid carrying the resistance gene was transferred by direct contact.
6.4.1–6.4.2 Protist Biology and Serial Endosymbiosis
  • Protists are highly heterogeneous eukaryotes — not grouped with plants, animals, or fungi.
  • Mostly unicellular; some colonial or simply multicellular. Predominantly aquatic or moist habitats.
  • Varied nutrition: autotrophs, heterotrophs, or mixotrophs (switch strategy depending on the environment).
  • Critical concept: "Protist" is NOT a valid clade — it is a paraphyletic convenience group. Animals, plants, and fungi are phylogenetically "nested" among the protists.
OrganelleAncestral bacterium (endosymbiosis)
MitochondrionAlpha-proteobacteria (aerobic)
ChloroplastCyanobacteria (oxygenic photosynthetics)

6 pieces of evidence for endosymbiosis (frequently tested):

  • Double membrane — the outer one comes from phagocytosis; the inner one is the original bacterial membrane.
  • Own circular DNA — similar to bacterial DNA, without histones like nuclear DNA.
  • 70S ribosomes — bacterial type, not 80S like the rest of the eukaryotic cell.
  • Division by binary fission — independent of host cell division.
  • Size — comparable to present-day bacteria.
  • DNA sequences — mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA group phylogenetically with specific bacteria.
🔬 Process — Origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts by endosymbiosis
  1. Large ancestral cell (proto-eukaryote / archaeal) capable of phagocytizing other cells.
  2. Phagocytizes an aerobic alpha-proteobacterium → instead of digesting it, keeps it alive inside.
  3. A mutually beneficial relationship is established: the bacterium provides ATP (aerobic respiration), the cell provides protection and nutrients.
  4. Over millions of years, the bacterium loses unnecessary genes, transfers its genetic material to the nucleus → becomes a mitochondrion.
  5. Later event: a eukaryotic cell already with mitochondria phagocytizes a photosynthetic cyanobacterium → same process → chloroplast.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Protist is an evolutionarily valid kingdom" → FALSE, it is a paraphyletic group.
• "All protists are microscopic" → FALSE. Brown algae (kelps) can reach 30+ m.
• "All organelles arose by endosymbiosis" → FALSE. Nucleus, ER, and Golgi arose by membrane invagination. Only mitochondria and chloroplasts have a clear endosymbiotic origin.
🧠 Scenario: A new organelle is discovered in a protist with a double membrane, circular DNA, and 70S ribosomes. What hypothesis arises? A: Endosymbiotic origin from a bacterium.
6.4.3–6.4.5 Ecological Role, Diversity, and Protist Groups
Ecological roleExamples
Aquatic producers (phytoplankton)Diatoms, dinoflagellates, green algae
Aquatic consumers (zooplankton)Ciliates, foraminifera
ParasitesPlasmodium (malaria), Trypanosoma (Chagas), Giardia
SymbiontsZooxanthellae in corals (build reefs)

Phytoplankton produces ≈ 50% of the world's atmospheric oxygen and is the base of marine food webs.

MotilityMechanismExample
CiliaShort, coordinated movementsParamecium
FlagellaLong whip-like movementsEuglena, Trypanosoma
PseudopodsCytoplasmic extensionsAmoebas
No evident locomotionSedentary forms or intracellular parasitesSome obligate parasites
Traditional groupCharacteristicsExamples
Animal-like (protozoa)Heterotrophic, motileAmoebas, ciliates, flagellates
Plant-like (algae)PhotosyntheticDiatoms, green, red, and brown algae
Fungus-likeHeterotrophic, absorptive, sporesSlime molds, water molds
⚠️ Trap: These groupings are practical, NOT phylogenetic. Modern systematics uses supergroups (Excavata, SAR, Archaeplastida, Amoebozoa). The course uses the traditional classification for simplicity.
6.5.1–6.5.2 Origin, Adaptations, and Alternation of Generations
  • Land plants evolved from ancestral green algae (charophytes) — they share chloroplasts with chlorophyll a and b, starch, and cellulose cell walls.
  • Central evolutionary challenge: colonization of the terrestrial environment posed problems that water solved "for free".
Land problemEvolutionary solution
DesiccationCuticle (impermeable waxy layer)
Gas exchange without water lossStomata with guard cells
Body support (without buoyancy)Lignin, vascular tissues
Internal transport of water and nutrientsXylem (water and minerals ↑) + Phloem (sugars in both directions)
Anchoring and soil absorptionRoots
Reproduction without free waterPollen, seeds
Dispersal of offspringFruits (angiosperms only)

Alternation of generations (fundamental concept):

PhasePloidyProduces
GametophyteHaploid (n)Gametes by mitosis
SporophyteDiploid (2n)Spores by meiosis
GroupDominant phaseWater dependence
BryophytesDominant gametophyteHigh — sperm must swim
Ferns (seedless vascular)Dominant sporophyteMedium — small but free gametophyte
Gymnosperms + AngiospermsHighly dominant sporophyte; gametophyte reduced to few cellsLow — pollen carries gametes without water
🔬 Process — Alternation of Generations (complete narrative)
  1. Begins with a haploid spore (n) that germinates and divides by mitosis → haploid multicellular gametophyte.
  2. The gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis (already haploid): sperm and eggs.
  3. Fertilization: fusion of gametes → diploid zygote (2n).
  4. The zygote divides by mitosis → diploid multicellular sporophyte.
  5. The sporophyte produces spores by meiosis in sporangia → haploid spores → cycle restarts.

Evolutionary trend: progressive reduction of the gametophyte and growing dominance of the sporophyte → less dependence on water for reproduction.

⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Bryophytes remain very tied to water for reproduction" → TRUE (reverse trap: confuse with gymnosperms).
• "All plants have the same level of terrestrial adaptation" → FALSE.
• "The gametophyte produces spores" → FALSE. The sporophyte produces spores (by meiosis); the gametophyte produces gametes (by mitosis).
🧠 Scenario: A plant has a large green gametophyte and a small sporophyte that grows on it and depends on it nutritionally. What group is it? A: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts).
6.5.3 Major Plant Taxonomic Groups
GroupVascular?Seed?Flower and fruit?Dominant phaseExamples
BryophytesNoNoNoGametophyteMosses, liverworts, hornworts
Seedless vascularYesNoNoSporophyteFerns, lycophytes, horsetails
GymnospermsYesYes (naked)NoSporophytePines, cypress, firs, sequoias
AngiospermsYesYes (in fruit)YesSporophyteOak, corn, apple tree, orchid

Each level = accumulated evolutionary innovation: 1) Vascular tissue → larger size. 2) Seed → reproduction without water + nutritional reserve. 3) Flower and fruit → targeted pollination + animal dispersal.

Exclusive innovations of angiosperms:

  • Double fertilization: one sperm → egg → embryo (2n); another → two polar nuclei → endosperm (3n).
  • Endosperm: triploid nutritive tissue (3n) that feeds the embryo. Gymnosperms do not have true endosperm.
  • Vessels in xylem (more efficient than the tracheids of gymnosperms).
🔬 Process — Double Fertilization in Angiosperms
  1. Pollen grain arrives at the stigma (by wind, insect, bird, bat).
  2. Pollen germinates → pollen tube grows through the style toward the ovary, carrying two sperm nuclei.
  3. The pollen tube reaches the ovule (embryo sac with egg cell + two polar nuclei).
  4. First fertilization: sperm nucleus + egg cell (n) → zygote (2n) → embryo.
  5. Second fertilization: second sperm nucleus + two polar nuclei → triploid nucleus (3n) → endosperm.
  6. Ovule → seed (embryo + endosperm + coat); ovary matures → fruit.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• GYMnosperms = GYMnosperm/naked seeds (without fruit). ANGIOsperms = seeds IN fruit.
• Confusing endosperm (3n, angiosperms) with nutritive tissue of gymnosperms (they are different things).
🧠 Scenario: If all angiosperms disappeared, what would happen to pollinators? A: Massive collapse. Most pollinators (bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, bats) depend on flowers. Gymnosperms (mostly wind-pollinated) cannot sustain them.
6.6.1–6.6.2 Characteristics and Life Cycle of Fungi
TraitFungiPlantsAnimals
NutritionHeterotrophic by absorptionAutotrophic (photosynthesis)Heterotrophic by ingestion
Cell wallYes, of chitinYes, of celluloseNone
BodyHyphae → myceliumTrue tissuesTrue tissues
Phylogenetic kinshipOpisthokontaArchaeplastidaOpisthokonta (closer to fungi than to plants)
  • Hypha: individual cellular filament (basic unit). Mycelium: interwoven network of hyphae (body of the fungus). Fruiting body (mushroom): visible reproductive structure — just the tip of the iceberg.
  • Types: saprotrophic (decompose dead matter), parasites (harm living host), mutualistic symbionts (beneficial exchange).

Fungal sexual cycle — unique dikaryotic phase in eukaryotes:

StageWhat happensPloidy
PlasmogamyFusion of cytoplasms of two compatible hyphaeNo nuclear fusion yet
Dikaryotic phaseTwo distinct haploid nuclei per cell (n + n). Can last yearsn + n (unusual)
KaryogamyFusion of the two nuclei → diploid cell2n
MeiosisReduces to haploid → sexual sporesn
🔬 Process — Fungal Sexual Life Cycle
  1. Two compatible hyphae ("+" and "−" types) come into contact.
  2. Plasmogamy: cytoplasms fuse; nuclei remain separate.
  3. Dikaryotic phase (n+n): two nuclei per cell; can last years in basidiomycetes.
  4. Fruiting body develops; in asci or basidia karyogamy occurs → transient diploid nucleus (2n).
  5. Meiosis → 4 haploid spores (ascospores or basidiospores).
  6. Spores disperse, germinate and form new haploid hyphae.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Fungi are plants" → FALSE. Chitin wall, heterotrophic by absorption, phylogenetically closer to animals.
• "Fertilization in fungi is the same as in animals" → FALSE. There is an intermediate dikaryotic phase (n+n) between plasmogamy and karyogamy.
• "All fungi reproduce sexually" → FALSE. Imperfect fungi (Deuteromycetes) only have known asexual reproduction.
6.6.3–6.6.4 Taxonomic Groups, Symbioses, and Ecological Importance
GroupDiagnostic traitsSexual structureExamples
ChytridsAquatic, flagellated spores (only group of fungi with flagella)VariousBatrachochytrium (kills amphibians)
ZygomycetesForm resistant zygosporesZygosporangiumBread molds (Rhizopus)
GlomeromycetesForm arbuscular mycorrhizae with most land plantsMostly asexualRoot symbionts
AscomycetesSexual spores inside an ascusAscus (ascospores)Yeasts, Penicillium, truffles, morels
BasidiomycetesSpores on a basidiumBasidium (basidiospores)Mushrooms, shelf fungi, rusts, smuts
SymbiosisWho participatesWhat the fungus contributesWhat the other contributes
MycorrhizaeFungus + plant rootGreater absorption of water and minerals (phosphorus)Sugars from photosynthesis
LichensFungus + green alga or cyanobacteriumStructure, protection, water retentionSugars from photosynthesis
  • Along with bacteria, fungi are the main decomposers of lignin and cellulose. Without them, forests would be buried in leaf litter.
  • Glomeromycetes were key in the original colonization of terrestrial environments by plants (~470 M years ago).
  • Lichens: pioneers in primary succession (grow on bare rock), initiate soil formation, air quality indicators.
  • Human importance: fermentation (bread, beer, wine) — yeasts; antibiotics — penicillin (Penicillium); food — mushrooms, blue cheeses; pathogens — candidiasis, ringworm.
⚠️ Trap: Reducing fungi to "decomposers". They are also essential symbionts, pathogens, industrial producers. | Confusing ascomycete/basidiomycete: ASCOspores in ASCIs / BASIDIOspores in BASIDIA.
🧠 Scenario: If a mycorrhiza dies completely in a forest region, what do you predict? A: Decrease in phosphorus and water absorption → plant stress → reduced growth → changes in community composition → cascade to herbivores and other trophic levels.
6.7.1–6.7.2 Animal Characteristics and Body Plan
  • Animals: multicellular heterotrophic eukaryotes, without cell wall, nutrition by ingestion, true tissues (except basal groups like sponges), complex embryonic development.
TraitTypesExamples
Germ layersDiploblastic (ecto + endo) / Triploblastic (+ mesoderm)Diploblastic: Cnidarians | Triploblastic: majority
SymmetryAsymmetric / Radial / BilateralSponges / Cnidarians, adult echinoderms / Most animals
CoelomAcoelomates / Pseudocoelomates / CoelomatesPlatyhelminthes / Nematodes / Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, chordates
SegmentationHomonymous (identical rings) / Heteronymous (tagmata)Annelids / Arthropods
CharacteristicProtostomesDeuterostomes
Fate of blastopore→ mouth→ anus
Embryonic cleavageSpiral and determinateRadial and indeterminate
Coelom formationSchizocoelicEnterocoelic
ExamplesMolluscs, annelids, arthropodsEchinoderms, chordates (humans)
🔬 Process — Gastrulation and Formation of Germ Layers
  1. Zygote → mitotic cleavages → morula (solid sphere) → blastula (hollow sphere with blastocoel).
  2. Gastrulation: cells invaginate → form archenteron (primitive gut), with opening called blastopore.
  3. Germ layers established: diploblastic (ecto + endo); triploblastic (+ mesoderm).
  4. Each layer gives rise to tissues: Ectoderm → epidermis, NS. Endoderm → digestive tract, lungs. Mesoderm → muscles, skeleton, circulatory system.
  5. Fate of blastopore defines lineage: Protostome = mouth; Deuterostome = anus.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Animals are defined by mobility" → FALSE. Adult sponges are sessile. Mobility may be only in the larva.
• "Echinoderms are simple animals far from humans" → FALSE. They are deuterostomes, closer to chordates than a worm or snail.
• "Invertebrate is an evolutionary clade" → FALSE. It is a paraphyletic group (everything that does NOT have a vertebral column).
🧠 Scenario: In an embryo, the blastopore becomes the anus. What lineage is it? A: Deuterostome → echinoderm or chordate.
6.7.3 Diagnostic Table of Invertebrates
PhylumSymmetryLayersCoelomExclusive / diagnostic traitExamples
PoriferaAsymmetricNo true tissues—Choanocytes + pore systemSponges
CnidariaRadialDiploblastic—Cnidocytes (stinging cells); two forms: polyp and medusaJellyfish, corals, hydras
PlatyhelminthesBilateralTriploblasticAcoelomatesFlattened body; incomplete digestion (single opening)Planarians, tapeworms, flukes
NematodaBilateralTriploblasticPseudocoelomatesCylindrical body, no segmentation, moulted cuticleAscaris, pinworms
MolluscaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomatesFoot + mantle + visceral mass; many with shell; radulaSnails, clams, octopuses
AnnelidaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomatesHomonymous segmentation (rings); setaeEarthworms, leeches, polychaetes
ArthropodaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomatesChitin exoskeleton + articulated appendages + moulting (ecdysis)Insects, arachnids, crustaceans
EchinodermataBilateral (larva) → Pentaradial (adult)TriploblasticCoelomatesWater vascular system + calcareous endoskeleton. DeuterostomesSea stars, sea urchins, sea cucumbers
  • Arthropods = most diverse animal group (~75% of described animal species are insects).
  • Echinoderms are deuterostomes → phylogenetically closer to chordates (humans) than to a worm or snail. Adult appearance is misleading.
⚠️ Traps: Only cnidarians have cnidocytes (if there's a stinging cell = cnidarian). | "Invertebrate" is not a clade: it's everything that does NOT have a vertebral column (paraphyletic). | Classifying by external appearance instead of deep embryological and anatomical traits.
🧠 Scenario: Aquatic bilateral animal, segmented, cylindrical, with setae on each segment. Which phylum? A: Annelid (polychaete if marine).
6.8.1–6.8.2 Characteristics of Chordates and Invertebrate Groups

Phylum Chordata. The 5 diagnostic traits may be present only in the embryo or larva, not necessarily in the adult:

Chordate traitFunction / Detail
NotochordFlexible dorsal support cord; in vertebrates replaced by vertebral column during development
Hollow dorsal nerve cordTubular central nervous system (in other animals the cord is ventral and solid)
Pharyngeal slitsIn aquatic forms: gills. In terrestrial tetrapods: only in embryo, modified into middle ear, neck, parathyroids
Post-anal tailMuscular extension beyond the anus (in humans only present in embryo → reduced to coccyx)
Endostyle (or thyroid in vertebrates)In invertebrate chordates: produces mucus for filter feeding. In vertebrates: evolved into the thyroid gland
Invertebrate groupCharacteristicsImportance
Urochordates (tunicates)Sessile adults, reduced chordate traits. Larvae clearly show notochord, dorsal nerve cord and post-anal tailTadpole-like larva: evidence of evolutionary relationship with vertebrates
Cephalochordates (amphioxus)Retain all chordate traits in the adult; fish-like body, without skullModel of the ancestral chordate body plan
⚠️ Traps:
• "Only vertebrates are chordates" → FALSE. Urochordates and cephalochordates are chordates without a vertebral column.
• "Chordate traits are always visible in the adult" → FALSE. In tunicates only the larva shows them clearly.
🧠 Scenario: A swimming larva with notochord and post-anal muscular tail becomes a sessile adult without those traits. What group is it? A: Urochordate (tunicate / ascidian).
6.8.3–6.8.4 Vertebrate Groups and Evolutionary Milestones
GroupKey traitsReproductionThermoregulationExamples
Agnatha (jawless fish)No jaw, cartilaginous skeletonAquaticEctothermLampreys, hagfish
Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fish)Jaw, cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scalesMostly oviparousEctothermSharks, rays
Osteichthyes (bony fish)Bony skeleton, operculum, swim bladderAquatic, mostly oviparousEctothermSalmon, tuna
AmphibiaBare moist skin, metamorphosisNeed water; unprotected eggsEctothermFrogs, salamanders
ReptiliaKeratinized scales, dry skin, amniote eggIndependent of waterEctothermTurtles, lizards, snakes
Aves (Birds)Feathers, hollow bones, amniote egg with hard shellOviparous; parental careEndothermEagles, penguins
MammaliaHair, mammary glands, 3 middle ear bones, diaphragmMostly viviparous; monotremes oviparousEndothermHumans, whales, platypus
Innovation (milestone)Problem solvedWho has it
JawsActive capture and processing of preyGnathostomes (all vertebrates except agnaths)
Limbs with digitsSupport and terrestrial locomotionTetrapods (amphibians + amniotes)
Amniote eggReproduction without free water; greater embryonic protectionReptiles, birds, mammals (amniotes)
EndothermySustained activity independent of ambient temperatureBirds and mammals (convergence — evolved twice)
  • "Fish" is not a valid clade: tetrapods descend from bony fish. In strict cladistics, humans are derived "sarcopterygian fish".
  • "Reptiles" is also not a clade: birds descend from theropod dinosaurs. The correct clade is Sauropsida (which includes birds).
  • Endothermy evolved independently in birds and in mammals (convergent evolution).
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "A fish becomes an amphibian that becomes a reptile" → FALSE. Evolution is branching, not a linear ladder.
• "Humans are the pinnacle of evolution" → FALSE. All current groups are equally modern temporally.
🧠 Scenario: If the amniote egg had never evolved, which groups would not exist? A: Reptiles, birds and mammals. Vertebrates would have remained limited to the vicinity of water for reproduction.
7
Topic 7 — Ecology
Populations, communities, energy flow and nutrients, main biosphere ecosystems
Summary
7.1.1–7.1.2 Ecology and Population Characteristics

Ecology: branch that studies the interactions of living beings with each other and with their environment. Organization hierarchy:

LevelWhat it includes
OrganismIndividual
PopulationIndividuals of a single species in an area and time
CommunityPopulations of several species in the same area
EcosystemCommunity + abiotic factors that interact
BiomeSet of similar ecosystems at large geographic scale
BiosphereAll life on Earth; set of all biomes
Population attributeWhat it describes
Size (N)Total number of individuals
DensityIndividuals per unit area or volume
Spatial distributionClumped (patches) | Uniform | Random
Age structureExpansive pyramid (growing) | Stable | Regressive (declining)
Demographic variablesΔN = (Birth rate + Immigration) − (Death rate + Emigration)
⚠️ Trap: "A meadow is not a population of grass" → it is a community (grass + insects + birds + microbiota) or an ecosystem if it includes the physical environment. | Confusing "population" with "species" or with "community".
7.1.3–7.1.4 Growth Models and Regulatory Factors
AspectExponential ModelLogistic Model
ResourcesUnlimitedLimited
Curve shapeJS (sigmoidal)
Is there K?NoYes — population slows as it approaches K
RealismLow; only short-term (invasion, recovery)High; closer to stable natural populations
Growth rateConstant (r)Decreases as it approaches K

K = Carrying capacity: maximum population size that the environment can sustainably support (determined by available water, food, space).

CharacteristicDensity-dependentDensity-independent
EffectIncreases as density increasesDoes not depend on how many individuals there are
NatureBiotic (mostly)Abiotic (mostly)
ExamplesCompetition, predation, diseases, parasitism, social stressDroughts, floods, fires, hurricanes, frosts
RoleTend to stabilize the population near KCause abrupt fluctuations independent of size
⚠️ Traps: Believe a population can grow exponentially forever → there is always K. | "All regulation is due to food shortage" → predation, diseases and social stress are also density-dependent.
🧠 Scenario: A fire eliminates 80% of deer. Wolves also decline. What factor affected each? A: Deer: density-independent factor (fire). Wolves: density-dependent factor (prey scarcity).
7.1.5–7.1.6 r and K Selection + Human Population
Characteristicr SelectionK Selection
Body sizeSmallLarge
Sexual maturityEarlyLate
OffspringMany, smallFew, large
Parental careMinimal or noneHigh and prolonged
Juvenile mortalityHighLow
Typical environmentUnstable, changing, disturbedStable, near K
Strategy"Bet on quantity""Bet on quality"
ExamplesBacteria, insects, weeds, mice, toadsElephants, whales, humans, trees, condors

Human population: K-extreme. Factors that accelerated growth: agriculture, medicine, sanitation, fossil energy → reduced mortality without proportionally reducing birth rates → recent exponential expansion.

  • Demographic transition: pre-industrial (high BR + high MR) → early industrial (high BR + low MR → explosion) → late industrial (low BR + low MR → stabilization) → post-industrial (possible decline).
  • Ecological impacts: intensive resource consumption, deforestation/urbanization, pollution, biodiversity loss, modification of biogeochemical cycles.
⚠️ Traps: r and K are extremes of a gradient — most species are at intermediate points. | Humans are NOT outside of ecological rules: technology extends K, but planetary resources are finite.
🧠 Scenario: A species produces thousands of eggs, doesn't care for them, juveniles mature in weeks and live only months. r or K selection? A: Typical r selection.
7.2.1–7.2.4 Structure, Niche, and Competition in Communities
  • Community = populations of different species in the same area. (Don't confuse with ecosystem, which also includes abiotic factors.)
  • Types of key species: Dominant species = very abundant, controls by biomass. Keystone species = not necessarily abundant, but its effect is disproportionate. Pioneer species = first to colonize disturbed areas.
ConceptWhat it describesAnalogy
HabitatWhere a species lives"Address"
Ecological nicheHow it lives, what it uses, what it tolerates, when it acts, how it interacts"Profession + lifestyle + address"
NicheDefinition
FundamentalWhere the species could live without interactions (theoretical potential)
RealizedWhere it actually lives after experiencing competition → always ≤ fundamental
Type of competitionDescriptionPossible consequence
IntraspecificAmong individuals of the same species; most intense at high densityDensity-dependent regulatory factor
InterspecificAmong different species with overlapping nichesCompetitive exclusion or resource partitioning
By exploitationConsume the same resource (no direct contact)Advantage to the most efficient
By interferenceOne directly prevents access of the other (aggression, territoriality)Displacement or forced coexistence

Gause's Principle: two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely → the one that better exploits the resource displaces the other (competitive exclusion). Coexistence requires differences in the niche.

⚠️ Traps: Niche ≠ habitat. | Dominant species ≠ keystone species (the keystone has enormous impact without necessarily being abundant). | Competition is not always physical aggression — it can be "use the resource first".
🧠 Scenario: Two birds in the same tree eat the same seeds, at the same time, on the same branch. What do you predict? A: Intense competition → in the long term competitive exclusion or resource partitioning (time, tree height, seed type).
7.2.5–7.2.7 Interactions, Structural Changes, and Succession
InteractionEffect AEffect BNotationExample
MutualismBenefitBenefit+ / +Pollinator and flower; mycorrhiza
CommensalismBenefitNo effect+ / 0Remora on shark
PredationBenefit (predator)Harm (death)+ / −Lion and zebra
HerbivoryBenefit (herbivore)Harm (plant)+ / −Cow and grass
ParasitismBenefit (parasite)Harm (no immediate death)+ / −Tick on dog
CompetitionHarmHarm− / −Two plants for light
AmensalismNo effectHarm0 / −Tree whose shade kills herbs below

Key difference: Predator usually kills immediately. Parasite typically does not kill immediately (lives at the expense of the host for a long time).

CharacteristicPrimary successionSecondary succession
Initial conditionWithout soil (bare rock, lava, retreated glacier)There was a community before; soil is preserved
SpeedVery slow (centuries or millennia)Faster (decades)
Typical pioneersLichens, mosses (no need for soil)Annual herbs, weeds
Typical causeVolcano, glacier, new duneFire, logging, abandoned cropland
  • Trophic cascade effect: changes at one level propagate to others. E.g.: removal of wolves (Yellowstone) → deer increase → overgrazing of willows → fewer beavers → change in waterways.
  • Lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium) are the pioneers of primary succession: dissolve rock with acids, initiate soil formation.
⚠️ Traps: "Primary succession" ≠ "secondary" → key is soil (secondary preserves it). | Succession does NOT always end in the same climax community (depends on climate, history, random events). | Reducing interactions to "predator and prey" — the exam usually asks for all 5-6 types with sign notation.
🧠 Scenario: Species A benefits, species B is not clearly affected. What interaction is it? A: Commensalism (+ / 0).
7.3.1–7.3.2 Ecosystem Dynamics and Energy Flow
ProcessCharacteristic
Energy flowUnidirectional — degrades to heat at each step; not recycled
Matter / nutrient cycleCyclic — elements are reused between organisms and environment
Trophic levelWhoExample (10,000 kcal base)
1st — ProducersPlants, algae, cyanobacteria (photosynthesis) or bacteria (chemosynthesis)10,000 kcal
2nd — Primary consumersHerbivores (cow, caterpillar)1,000 kcal
3rd — Secondary consumersPrimary carnivores (toad, wolf)100 kcal
4th — Tertiary consumersApex carnivores (eagle, shark)10 kcal

10% Rule: only ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; ~90% is lost as heat (metabolism, respiration, excretion). This is why energy pyramids always decrease and food chains rarely exceed 4-5 levels.

⚠️ Traps:
• "Energy is recycled like matter" → FALSE. Energy flows unidirectionally and is lost as heat.
• "Photosynthesis is the only energy input" → FALSE. Chemosynthesis provides energy in light-free ecosystems (deep-sea hydrothermal vents).
🧠 Scenario: Why are there fewer eagles than mice in an ecosystem? A: 10% rule. Mice receive ~10% of plant energy; eagles receive only ~10% of mouse energy. Less energy available at high trophic levels.
7.3.3–7.3.4 Primary Productivity and Biogeochemical Cycles
ConceptWhat it measures
GPP (Gross Primary Productivity)Total energy captured by producers (photosynthesis or chemosynthesis)
Producer respiration (R)Energy that the producers themselves use to live
NPP = GPP − REnergy stored as new biomass: available for herbivores and the rest of the ecosystem

Productivity by biome: Tropical rainforest >> temperate forest > savanna > taiga > grassland > tundra >> desert

Nitrogen cycle (most tested):

ProcessWhat it doesWho performs it
FixationAtmospheric N₂ → NH₄⁺ (assimilable form)Rhizobium (legume nodules), cyanobacteria, free Azotobacter
NitrificationNH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter
AssimilationNO₃⁻ or NH₄⁺ → proteins and nucleic acidsPlants (then passes to food chain)
AmmonificationNitrogenous organic matter → NH₄⁺Decomposers (bacteria and fungi)
DenitrificationNO₃⁻ → N₂ (returns to air)Anaerobic denitrifying bacteria
  • C cycle: photosynthesis (CO₂ → organic) ↔ respiration and decomposition (organic → CO₂). Fossil fuels = carbon stored millions of years ago, massively released by human combustion.
  • P cycle: no significant gas phase. Main reservoir: rocks. Slow release by weathering. Depletes in soils with intensive farming → reason for phosphate fertilizer use.
  • Decomposers are essential in ALL cycles: they release nutrients trapped in dead biomass.
🔬 Process — Carbon Cycle (complete narrative)
  1. Photosynthesis: plants/algae/cyanobacteria fix atmospheric CO₂ into organic biomass.
  2. Carbon flows through the food chain (herbivores → carnivores).
  3. Cellular respiration (all organisms): organic → CO₂ to air.
  4. Decomposition (fungi + bacteria): dead biomass → CO₂.
  5. Some carbon becomes trapped for millions of years in fossil fuels (organic matter without decomposition in anaerobic conditions).
  6. Oceans: CO₂ dissolves ↔ bicarbonates (continuous exchange).
  7. Human impact: fossil combustion and deforestation release carbon accumulated over millions of years → CO₂ accumulation → global warming.
⚠️ Traps: GPP ≠ NPP — if asked "energy available for herbivores" = NPP. | Atmospheric nitrogen (78% of air) is inaccessible without fixing bacteria. | P cycle has no gas phase. | Energy flows; matter cycles — they are not the same.
🧠 Scenario: If all decomposers disappear, what happens? A: Nutrients become trapped in dead biomass. Plants cannot access recycled N, P, C. Productivity collapses within a few years.
7.3.5–7.3.6 Human Disturbance and Climate Change
CycleHuman activityConsequence
CarbonFossil combustion, deforestationCO₂ accumulation → global warming, ocean acidification
NitrogenNitrogen fertilizers, combustion, livestockRunoff → eutrophication, "dead zones"
PhosphorusPhosphate fertilizers, detergentsEutrophication; depletion of mineral reserves
WaterOverexploitation, dams, alteration of waterwaysWater stress, salinization, loss of wetlands

Eutrophication (key process for exam):

🔬 Process — Eutrophication Step by Step
  1. Excess N and P reach the water body (fertilizers, wastewater).
  2. Algae and cyanobacteria proliferate massively (algal bloom).
  3. The surface layer blocks light → submerged aquatic plants die.
  4. Algae die in mass and sink to the bottom.
  5. Aerobic decomposers consume the dissolved O₂ in the water.
  6. Hypoxic or anoxic zone at the bottom → fish and invertebrates die from asphyxia.
  7. Result: "dead zone" (e.g., Gulf of Mexico, Baltic Sea).
Climate change effectEcological consequence
Temperature increaseSpecies shift to higher latitudes/altitudes
Changes in phenologyDesynchronization between pollinators, prey and predators
Permafrost thawingRelease of CO₂ and methane (positive feedback) → more warming
Ocean acidificationDissolved CO₂ lowers pH → damage to corals and calcified-shell organisms
⚠️ Trap: "Climate change is just more heat" → FALSE. It also alters precipitation, cycles, habitat distribution, extreme events, ocean chemistry. | Studying cycles as "closed" processes without including human impact.
🧠 Scenario: A plant flowers 2 weeks earlier due to warming, but its pollinator doesn't advance its migration. What do you predict? A: Phenological desynchronization → plant not efficiently pollinated → reproduction declines → pollinator loses its resource. Disruption of mutualism due to climate change.
7.4.1–7.4.3 Biosphere, Climate, and Terrestrial Biomes

Biosphere: set of all the Earth's ecosystems. Climate (combination of temperature, precipitation, latitude, altitude and atmospheric circulation) is the main determinant of biome distribution.

BiomeClimatePrecipitationDominant vegetationProductivity
Tropical rainforestWarm and humid year-round>200 cm/yearDense layered trees, epiphytes, lianasVery high
SavannaWarm with marked dry season50–150 cm/yearTall grasses + scattered treesMedium-high
DesertWarm or cold; very dry<25 cm/yearSparse plants, succulents, extensive rootsVery low
Grassland / steppeSeasonal temperate25–75 cm/yearDominant grasses, few treesMedium (high agricultural yield)
Temperate forestTemperate with 4 seasons75–150 cm/yearDeciduous trees (oak, maple, beech)Medium-high
Taiga / boreal forestCold, long wintersLow-moderateConifers (pines, firs)Medium-low
TundraVery cold, permafrostVery lowMosses, lichens, dwarf grassesVery low
  • Tropical rainforest: paradoxically nutrient-poor soil (nutrients are in living biomass; very fast recycling). Richness is in trees, not in soil.
  • Grassland: deep fertile soils → world's breadbaskets (corn, wheat, soy). Natural fires maintain grass dominance.
  • Tundra: permafrost (permanently frozen subsoil) prevents deep roots and limits decomposition → stores large amounts of carbon that climate change can release (positive feedback).
⚠️ Traps:
• "Tropical rainforest has rich soils" → FALSE. Nutrients are in biomass, not soil (quickly lost when deforested).
• "A single factor (soil, temperature) determines biome distribution" → FALSE. It's the combination of climatic factors that defines it.
• Memorizing biome names without associating them with climate and productivity.
🧠 Scenario: If a savanna receives much higher and constant rainfall, toward what biome would it tend to transform? A: Toward a tropical forest (high temperature) or temperate forest (lower temperature). More humidity allows dense trees and displaces grasses.
7.4.4–7.4.5 Aquatic Ecosystems, Threats, and Sustainable Development
CategorySubcategoriesKey factorsSpecial note
FreshwaterRivers and streams (lotic)Current, O₂, substrateHighly oxygenated due to movement
Lakes and ponds (lentic)Depth, light, stratificationCan stratify by temperature
WetlandsWater periodicityHigh productivity and biodiversity
MarineOpen oceanLight, depth, temperaturePhotic zone (0–200m) vs aphotic (>200m)
Coral reefsWarm, clear, shallow watersHighest biodiversity per area of any marine habitat
Coastal / intertidal zonesTides, variable salinityOrganisms tolerant to desiccation and wave action
EstuariesChanging salinity (river + sea)Very productive; fish nurseries

Photic vs aphotic zone: Photic (~0–200m): light present, photosynthesis, producers. Aphotic (>200m): no light, depends on "marine snow" (organic matter falling from above) or chemosynthesis (abyssal hydrothermal vents → bacteria using H₂S).

Threat (HIPPO)DescriptionExample
Habitat destructionConversion of natural ecosystems for human useAmazonian deforestation, wetland urbanization
Invasive speciesDisplace native speciesBullfrog, feral cats and dogs on islands
PollutionHarmful substances in air, water, soilPesticides, heavy metals, microplastics
OverexploitationUse at rates exceeding replacementOverfishing, illegal hunting, selective logging
Climate changeLong-term alteration of conditionsWarming, ocean acidification

Sustainable development (3 pillars): 1) Environmental: maintain ecosystem integrity. 2) Social: equity and human well-being. 3) Economic: productive systems that do not destroy their ecological base.

  • Biodiversity loss → loss of ecosystem services (pollination, pest control, water purification, soil fertility) and ecological resilience.
⚠️ Trap: "All aquatic ecosystems work the same because they all have water" → FALSE. The differences between an estuary and the deep ocean are enormous. | "Sustainable development = using fewer things" → FALSE. It requires integrated ecological, social, and economic planning.
🧠 Scenario: At abyssal hydrothermal vents no sunlight reaches them, yet dense communities exist. How? A: Chemosynthesis. Bacteria use H₂S as an energy source, forming the base of the food chain. Ecology independent of the sun.
📖 Master Glossary — U3 100+ terms · quick search

🔬 Biological Diversity — Topic 6

TermWorking definition
Viral adsorptionFirst stage of the viral cycle: the virus binds to specific receptors on the host cell.
Alternation of generationsPlant life cycle with two alternating multicellular phases: gametophyte (n) and sporophyte (2n).
AnalogyStructure with similar function but different evolutionary origin.
ArchaeaDomain of prokaryotes without peptidoglycan, with membrane lipids containing ether bonds.
Ascus / ascosporeSexual structure in ascomycetes; spore produced inside an ascus.
BacteriophageVirus that infects bacteria.
Basidium / basidiosporeSexual structure in basidiomycetes; spore produced on a basidium.
CapsidProtein coat of a virus.
KaryogamyFusion of nuclei in fungi, following plasmogamy.
CephalizationConcentration of sensory and nervous structures in the anterior region of the body.
CoelomBody cavity completely surrounded by mesoderm.
CladeGroup that includes a common ancestor and all its descendants (monophyletic).
CnidocyteStinging cell exclusive to cnidarians; contains nematocysts.
ChoanocyteCell with flagellum and collar; exclusive to porifera (sponges).
Bacterial conjugationDirect DNA transfer between bacteria through a sex pilus.
ChordatesPhylum defined by notochord, hollow dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail, and endostyle.
CuticleWaxy impermeable layer of terrestrial plants that reduces water loss.
DeuterostomeAnimal whose blastopore becomes the anus; examples: echinoderms and chordates.
Double fertilizationProcess exclusive to angiosperms: one sperm forms the zygote (2n), another forms the endosperm (3n).
Serial endosymbiosisTheory explaining the origin of mitochondria (from alpha-proteobacteria) and chloroplasts (from cyanobacteria).
EndosporeBacterial resistance structure capable of surviving extreme conditions.
EndothermyAbility to maintain a high, stable body temperature through internal metabolism.
StomaPlant pore with guard cells that regulates gas exchange.
EukaryaDomain of organisms with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
PhylogenyEvolutionary history of a group of organisms.
Binary fissionProkaryotic asexual reproduction; division into two identical daughter cells.
GametophyteHaploid phase (n) of the plant cycle; produces gametes by mitosis.
GnathostomesVertebrates with jaws.
Gram positive / negativeBacterial classification by Gram stain reaction; reflects differences in cell wall structure.
Pharyngeal slitsOpenings in the pharynx; diagnostic trait of chordates.
HyphaCellular filament of the fungal body; basic unit.
HomologyStructure with common evolutionary origin, possibly with a different function.
Amniote eggEgg with protective membranes (amnion, chorion, allantois) enabling terrestrial reproduction.
LichenSymbiosis between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium.
Lysogenic cycleViral cycle in which the genome integrates as a prophage and the cell survives.
Lytic cycleViral cycle in which the virus actively replicates and lyses the cell.
MesodermIntermediate germ layer in triploblasts; origin of muscles, skeleton, and blood.
MyceliumNetwork of hyphae that forms the fungal body.
MycorrhizaSymbiosis between a fungus and a plant root.
MixotrophOrganism that combines autotrophy and heterotrophy depending on conditions.
NotochordFlexible dorsal support rod in chordates.
Cell wallRigid outer covering; peptidoglycan in bacteria, chitin in fungi, cellulose in plants.
PeptidoglycanPolymer exclusive to the bacterial cell wall.
PlasmogamyFusion of cytoplasms in fungi, without immediate nuclear fusion.
PrionMisfolded protein that induces misfolding in other proteins.
ProphageViral genome integrated into the host chromosome during the lysogenic cycle.
ProtostomeAnimal whose blastopore becomes the mouth; examples: mollusks, annelids, arthropods.
ChitinPolymer of the fungal cell wall and arthropod exoskeleton.
Binomial nomenclatureScientific naming: genus + specific epithet.
SystematicsIntegrated study of diversity and evolutionary relationships.
TaxonAny group recognized in the taxonomic hierarchy.
TetrapodVertebrate with four limbs.
TransductionBacteriophage-mediated bacterial genetic transfer.
TransformationUptake of free DNA from the environment by a bacterium.
ViroidNaked circular RNA, without capsid; infects plants.
VirusAcellular entity with genetic material (DNA or RNA) and a protein capsid.

🌿 Ecology — Topic 7

TermWorking definition
Amensalism0/− interaction: one species is unaffected, the other is harmed.
AmmonificationDecomposers convert organic nitrogenous compounds into NH₄⁺.
Assimilation (N)Incorporation of nitrates or ammonium into organic molecules by plants.
BiomeSet of similar ecosystems at a large geographic scale.
BiosphereThe sum of all ecosystems on Earth.
Carrying capacity (K)Maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely.
Trophic cascadeChain effect where changes at one trophic level ripple through others.
Commensalism+/0 interaction: one species benefits, the other is unaffected.
CommunitySet of populations of different species in an area.
Competition−/− interaction: both species are harmed by use of a shared resource.
Density-dependentRegulatory factor whose effect intensifies with population density (e.g., disease).
Density-independentFactor that affects the population regardless of its density (e.g., droughts, fires).
Predation+/− interaction: the predator benefits, the prey is harmed/killed.
DenitrificationBacterial conversion of NO₃⁻ to gaseous N₂ under anaerobic conditions.
EcosystemCommunity + abiotic factors in a location.
Keystone speciesSpecies with disproportionate impact relative to its abundance.
EutrophicationNutrient enrichment → algal bloom → O₂ depletion → dead zone.
PhenologyTiming of cyclic biological events (flowering, migration, reproduction).
Nitrogen fixationConversion of atmospheric N₂ to usable forms (NH₃/NH₄⁺) by bacteria.
HabitatPhysical place where a species lives.
Logistic modelPopulation growth with carrying capacity; sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve.
Mutualism+/+ interaction: both species benefit.
Ecological nicheComplete functional role of a species: resources, conditions, interactions.
Fundamental nicheSet of conditions where the species could theoretically live.
Realized nicheSet of conditions where it actually lives after interactions.
NitrificationBacterial oxidation of NH₄⁺ to NO₂⁻ and then to NO₃⁻.
Parasitism+/− interaction: the parasite benefits, the host is harmed without immediate death.
PermafrostPermanently frozen soil; stores large amounts of carbon.
PopulationIndividuals of the same species in the same area and time.
Gause's PrincipleTwo species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely.
Gross Primary Productivity (GPP)Total energy captured by producers.
Net Primary Productivity (NPP)GPP minus producer respiration; energy available to herbivores.
ChemosynthesisSynthesis of organic molecules using chemical energy (not light).
10% Rule~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; ~90% is lost as heat.
K selectionStrategy: few offspring, extensive parental care, long life.
r selectionStrategy: many offspring, little parental care, short life.
Primary successionCommunity change from a substrate with no prior soil.
Secondary successionCommunity change after a disturbance that preserves the soil.
TaigaBoreal coniferous forest biome.
TundraVery cold biome with permafrost and low-lying vegetation.
Photic zoneSurface aquatic layer with enough light for photosynthesis.
